#815. Golloria Responds to Huda Beauty’s Apology for Removing Darkest Powder

Beauty influencer Golloria responded to Huda Beauty founder Huda Kattan's apology for how the company handled removing its darkest setting powder Coffee Cake and replacing it with Coco Truffle.

Golloria can’t conceal her thoughts on Huda Beauty’s apology.

After the makeup brand’s founder Huda Kattan apologized to the beauty influencer for how her company handled discontinuing their darkest setting powder Coffee Cake and replacing it with Coco Truffle, Golloria shared her thoughts on the response.

“I appreciate your apology and you taking the time to get back to me,” Golloria posted in the comments of Kattan’s Nov. 20 Instagram post. “Speaking from both my experience as a shade consultant and as a dark skinned woman whose shade options are directly affected by this decision, I don’t think Coco Truffle should replace Coffee Cake. And that’s just the honest truth.”

The TikToker explained that she heard Huda Beauty’s reasoning that Coffee Cake wasn’t doing well with consumers, but added that she didn’t think the two shades were “interchangeable,” noting that “a shade occupying a similar depth in a range doesn’t necessarily mean it serves the same complexions.”

“You’ve said several times that you want to better serve dark skinned women, and part of that is listening to the women telling you that Coffee Cake already works for them,” the 25-year-old continued. “That feedback should help guide what you preserve as you expand the range.”

She also added that darker skinned women “deserve variety in both depth and undertone,” and that having both shades would help create that inclusion. Instead, Golloria shared in her own Instagram caption that she felt Huda Beauty was “doing what's easiest for the brand instead of what's needed by the women you say you want to serve.”

“Inclusion means making room for our differences,” she wrote, “not asking us to settle for whatever is most convenient for you to offer.”

As for Kattan, while the beauty founder did not reply to Golloria’s comment, she explained in her apology video that she was sorry for how the conversation about the shade replacement had been handled with Golloria, especially as it was happening during a busy time for the brand and when Kattan herself had to undergo emergency surgery for a ruptured breast implant in April.

According to the 43-year-old, her team found that Coffee Cake was “not something that a lot of people have shared positive feedback with us on,” adding that they “definitely thought we could make it a lot better.”

The decision led them to launching Coco Truffle as a replacement for Coffee Cake, first as a pressed powder, then as a loose powder—although it was not yet widely available.. But after hearing from their consumers, Kattan realized they should have done a better job being more inclusive with their shades.

“Inclusivity is not about, ‘Yes, done, check, we're inclusive.’ That to me is some of the things that are wrong with the industry,” she said. “It's 2026. We can do better. We can do better and I think brands should be doing better in 2026.”

And while they will be reworking Coco Truffle to make sure it’s available “as quickly as possible,” she also regretted fully removing Coffee Cake from their lineup.

“We should have kept it in stores,” Kattan said, “because at the end of the day, if some people liked it, we should have kept it in stores until there was something better available.”

She also once again apologized for not having better communicated all of this to Golloria initially, although she was hopeful that the beauty influencer and Huda Beauty fans would appreciate Coco Truffle.

“I'm hoping to give you guys a shade that you guys really, really love, and all the beautiful rich skin tone girls and boys feel really represents them,” Kattan shared, “and is perfect for their skin tone.”

It comes down to choices made for speed and science, as the two spacecraft flew by planets in the 1970s and 1980s.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Voyager 1 is about to reach a light-day of distance in space, but Voyager 2 won't hit the mark until about 2035. Why the big difference?

On Nov. 18, Voyager 1 will be so far away from Earth that it will take a full light-day (24 hours) to send a signal to the distant spacecraft, at 16,094,799,096 miles (25,902,068,356 kilometers). Since light is essentially the maximum speed in the universe (absent using devices like wormholes, or quantum-physics puzzles), it's a big deal — so big that NASA will be celebrating the milestone by asking fans to shine Morse Code signals at the sky.

But why will Voyager 2 take nearly a decade longer? It comes down to choices made for speed and science during the twin missions' nearly 50-year journey, specifically during the first bit when they were flying by planets. The result is Voyager 1 is zooming out at a speed of 3.5 Earth-sun distances (astronomical units a year), while Voyager 2 has a more stately speed of 3.1 Earth-sun distances, according to NASA.

The original aim of both the spacecraft, which launched about two weeks apart in 1977 with Voyager 2 going first, was to look at Jupiter and Saturn. If funding persisted, which it did, the hope was to bring Voyager 2 past Uranus and Neptune, taking advantage of a rare planetary alignment. Voyager 1, by contrast, made a turn at Saturn to look at the planet's rings and the prebiotic (pre-life-chemistry) moon of Titan, before flying outside the plane of the solar system.

NASA had a range of trajectory options to consider when launching the spacecraft, and elected to bring Voyager 1 at a faster trajectory — as illustrated in this video by Britannica, where you can quickly see the spacecraft overtaking Voyager 2 on its way to Jupiter even though Voyager 1. Voyager 1 arrived at Jupiter on March 5, 1979 while Voyager 2 got there four months later on July 9.

Each of the spacecraft then performed a "gravity assist"—a sort of slingshot around the planet in which they took a tiny bit of momentum from Jupiter to gain speed as the spacecraft flew to Saturn. This technique is used constantly, such as recently when the ESCAPADE Mars mission flew two spacecraft by Earth on the way to the Red Planet, as it allows spacecraft to gain speed while saving on fuel. The planets themselves don't slow down that much.

"Because the planet is so much more massive than the spacecraft, the transfer doesn't affect the planet to any measurable extent, but to the spacecraft it's a big deal," the Planetary Society wrote. "For example, we can calculate that during the Voyager encounters with Jupiter in 1979, Jupiter slowed down by roughly 10 to the -24th power kilometers per second — a change much too small to measure."

"But each Voyager gained about 10 km/s [6.2 miles/s], a pretty big number," the society continued about the Jupiter encounter. This was "enough to put them on a fast path to Saturn — and in the case of Voyager 2, to Uranus and Neptune as well — and eventual escape from the solar system."

With each flyby, the two spacecraft picked up speed with a single exception — during Voyager 2's encounter of Neptune. That's because the spacecraft made a turn to fly by Triton. The maneuver brought Voyager 2 over Neptune's north pole, before it turned and then was directed to begin "plunging down, out of the plane of the solar system," losing speed along the way.

Voyager 2, in fact, did not have enough speed to leave the solar system until it flew by Jupiter. "It gained about 10 km/s at Jupiter, about 5 km/s at Saturn, about 2 km/s at Uranus, and lost about 2 km/s at Neptune," the Planetary Society wrote of the speeds, which are 6.21 miles/s, 3.11 miles/s, 1.24 miles/s and a loss of 1.24 miles/s, respectively.

At any rate, these fast speeds allowed both spacecraft not only to go fast, but to eventually reach interstellar space in 2012 (Voyager 1) and 2018 (Voyager 2), respectively. With the light-day milestone now reached by Voyager 1, it is anticipated the spacecraft could work into the 2030s, as long as their nuclear power sources can last.

NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, which manages the mission, has been carefully turning off instruments as required, and recently did a "Big Bang" procedure on both spacecraft to redistribute power supplies as best as possible. The idea is to maximize science return on both spacecraft, the only interstellar messengers we have, for as long as possible.

Elizabeth Howell (she/her), Ph.D., was a staff writer in the spaceflight channel between 2022 and 2024 specializing in Canadian space news. She was contributing writer for Space.com for 10 years from 2012 to 2024. Elizabeth's reporting includes multiple exclusives with the White House, leading world coverage about a lost-and-found space tomato on the International Space Station, witnessing five human spaceflight launches on two continents, flying parabolic, working inside a spacesuit, and participating in a simulated Mars mission. Her latest book, "Why Am I Taller?" (ECW Press, 2022) is co-written with astronaut Dave Williams.

#810. DW Science explainer on the default mode network: what your brain does when you aren't focusing on anything, and why it's important.

Doing nothing might be the ultimate brain hack. When you're bored, the brain goes into default mode network. It's not only healthy for you, but it may also shape the very essence of your identity.

You know when you lock your phone and the screen goes black? It seems like it's not doing anything. But it's not doing nothing. It's syncing your messages, updating apps and running other background processes.

Imagine you're sitting on a bus, staring out of a window, taking a shower or walking, and you get that feeling of doing nothing and letting your mind drift?

Well, your mind, the brain, is doing a lot when it feels like you're doing nothing.

It's going over your memories, shaping your sense of who you are, imagining possible futures, helping you understand other people and connecting ideas.

That's your brain's default mode network.

Scientists conducted brain-imaging experiments in the 1990s and early 2000s to find out which regions of the brain were active during demanding tasks, like solving a math problem or memory exercise.

But to measure that, they needed a so-called baseline. They needed to know the level of brain activity at rest and during demanding tasks.

So, between the tasks, they asked participants to relax, close their eyes, stare at a fixed point on a wall, or try not to think of anything at all.

And they measured the participants' brain activity both when they were solving a task and doing nothing. That's how scientists noticed the brain was active in up- and downtime.

They noticed that when participants started to focus on a new task, after having done nothing, some brain areas lit up and other areas dimmed down. That suggests those areas that dimmed down must have been active while the participant was apparently — physically and mentally — at rest.

This realization eventually led to the discovery of the default mode network or DMN.

The DMN is crucial because it helps your brain make sense of your life and experiences.

It helps you connect and revisit memories, reflect on who you are, imagine what might happen in future scenarios, understand other people, build meaning from experience, and connect ideas in new ways.

It turns all your memories, experiences, knowledge, emotions and social information into your internal story. Think of that story as a constantly evolving, updated model of who you are and how you engage with the world around you.

But it's important to understand the DMN involves more than one area of the brain. It is a group of brain regions that light up when you're not focused on an external task.

There's another player in your brain that acts as a monitoring system. You can think of it as constantly asking "Is there anything that needs my attention?"

Imagine you're daydreaming while driving, and a car suddenly swerves into your lane.

In a fraction of a second, your daydream disappears and your attention snaps back to the road. That player is called the salience network, or SN.

The salience network helps you notice important signals, like a sound, a mistake, pain, an emotion, a threat, or something happening in your body, and helps shift the brain toward attention and control systems when action is needed.

The DMN, SN and attention/control systems constantly interact.

And the DMN doesn't just turn off completely with every hard task. Parts of it can also contribute when tasks involve memory, stories, meaning or other people.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Smartphones have filled many of the small empty moments of our days — waiting for the bus, standing in line, eating alone, lying on the couch. We are constantly looking at our devices.

So, it seems reasonable to ask: are we crowding out those moments of boredom where DMN kicks in?

Maybe. But so far, there's no strong evidence that scrolling directly affects mental health by reducing DMN time.

What we do know is that problematic smartphone use can increase stress, anxiety, task-switching and disrupt sleep.

And sleep loss and stress also have clearer evidence for altering DMN-related brain connectivity.

When your mind wanders, it might produce a great new idea.

But it might also replay an embarrassing thing you did five years ago. Again. And again.

In depression, the self-reflection part of the DMN can get caught in repetitive negative loops that are hard to stop — what's known as rumination.

Scientists have also found that Alzheimer's disease targets key DMN areas, particularly those responsible for your autobiographical memory and remembering other aspects of the past. Which may help explain why memory problems are so central to the disease.

Protect your sleep and take stress seriously. There is direct evidence that sleep loss and stress disrupt DMN-related connectivity.

Take real, quiet breaks after mentally demanding tasks, like studying. It can even help you memorize facts for your exam.

Try to reframe boredom as this essential, energy-intensive active work in your brain that builds your internal narrative and sense of self, consolidates memories, creates connections and sparks creativity.

Try waiting in line without checking your phone. Look out the window next time you take the bus or take a walk without listening to anything.

You can also try scheduling DMN time. It may be the closest thing to a real brain hack.

It now takes 24 hours for even a single particle of light to reach Voyager.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft is now one light-day from Earth — so far away that it takes signals a full 24 hours to reach the probe.

Voyager 1 launched on Sept. 5, 1977, just a couple of weeks after Voyager 2 lifted off. But Voyager 1 launched on a faster trajectory than its twin and has just become the first spacecraft to ever reach one light-day away, which is equivalent to about 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers), or the distance that one light particle travels in 24 hours. The milestone — which Voyager 1 hit today (Nov. 18) at 5:16 a.m. EST (1016 GMT) — shows the incredible ingenuity, technical ability and creativity from the teams at NASA that continue to innovate to keep this mission going nearly five decades later.

"The Earth and Voyager are exactly 24 hours apart at the speed of light," Voyager Project Scientist Linda Spilker told Space.com. "It's a very special moment where Voyager 1 is about 16.1 billion miles away, and we're celebrating that moment because it's the first human-made object to actually reach one light-day distance."

The two Voyager spacecraft have been on one serious ride since launching in 1977. And each of these twin probes has taken a unique and historic journey through our solar system and beyond.

On Voyager 1's trip through our cosmic neighborhood, for example, it made countless groundbreaking observations of planets and moons that we had never before seen up close (or at all). The probe discovered a ring around Jupiter as well as the planet's moons Thebe and Metis. It also found five new moons and a new ring around Saturn.

"Voyager 1 flew past the Jupiter system and took images of Jupiter's moon Io, and it actually discovered that Io is volcanically active. So, images that were taken showed these volcanoes that were actively erupting, and we learned that Io is actually the most volcanically active body in our solar system, which is just amazing," Cynthia Phillips, a project scientist for NASA's Europa Clipper mission, told Space.com about one of Voyager 1's many discoveries.

"And then, as Voyager 1 continued out to the Saturn system, it actually discovered that Saturn's large moon Titan has a very thick atmosphere surrounding it," she added. "So it's one of the only moons that has a thick atmosphere."

Decades later, Voyager 1's data is still incredibly important for scientists studying the planets and moons of our cosmic neighborhood. Phillips works on Clipper, which is on its way to study Jupiter's ocean moon Europa. And the basis of that work stems from early observations by Voyager.

"Every time I get to use data from Voyager, I have to kind of think back to where that data came from," Phillips said. "I think about kind of the legacy, the missions that really set the precedent for a mission like Europa Clipper. Voyager is right there at the top of the list. And some of those images that we took with the Voyager 1 and 2 spacecraft of Europa — they're actually still, for some portions of Europa, they're the best pictures that we have. So, we're still using that data today, almost 50 years later."

Today, Voyager 1 and 2 are both exploring interstellar space. On Aug. 25, 2012, Voyager 1 became the first human-made object to leave the heliosphere, or the protective bubble of solar particles that surrounds the planets and other objects in our solar system. After crossing that boundary, Voyager 1 entered interstellar space and has been exploring the interstellar medium ever since. Voyager 2 followed suit in November 2018.

While the Voyager spacecraft have left the heliosphere, they have technically not left the solar system, as they are still within the gravitational influence of the sun. Today, Voyager 1 is traveling 38,000 mph (61,155 kph) through interstellar space, exploring farther than any human-made object in history.

The Voyager mission team communicates with Voyager in radio waves via the Deep Space Network, a collective of giant radio antennas that NASA uses to "talk" to a wide range of far-off spacecraft. And since radio waves travel at the speed of light, it now takes 24 hours for communications to reach Voyager 1, and then another 24 hours for any response to return.

"You need to have patience because now, if you send a command to Voyager, Voyager receives that command 24 hours later," Spilker said. "So two days later, you receive confirmation that yes, Voyager one received your command and is sending back the information that you'd like it to send back."

That patience is important, as the nearly-50-year-old Voyager mission is still actively making science observations and collecting new data. While some of the probes' science instruments have had to be shut off over the years to save battery life, both probes are still going strong.

"It is always difficult when an instrument has to get turned off, knowing that it has returned good science data for so many years," Spilker said. "But a plan was laid down to make sure we had at least one instrument operating on each spacecraft, one type of instrument, for as long as we could."

As long as the mission is active, the team will continue to investigate the unknown with Voyager. After all, ever since the probes entered interstellar space, they have been exploring areas of space that we've only ever studied remotely or in theory.

"Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause in 2012, and what we knew about interstellar space at that point really came just from remote observations and theories. And so, right away, Voyager started to find that what we expected was not exactly right," Spilker said.

So far, the team has found that the sun's influence extends much farther from the heliopause than they expected. The Voyagers have observed and measured "ripples coming from the sun," as Spilker described them, deep in interstellar space.

"Voyager is going to continue to measure the cosmic rays and particles, and also the radio waves coming from interstellar space and coming from the sun," Spilker said, adding that the team is always eagerly "waiting to see if there might be more surprises out there."

How has this mission from the 1970s continued to not just survive but actively push forward through all of that time, overcoming countless hurdles and unexpected challenges?

"Voyager's longevity is really a tribute to all of the people who worked on Voyager, from those who designed the spacecraft, built it, programmed its computers, launched it, and then the teams of individuals that have flown it over that 50 years," Spilker said.

Spilker is a longtimeVoyager veteran. Fresh out of school, she started her NASA career with Voyager, working on the mission for about a decade before moving on to NASA's Cassini Saturn mission. After Cassini concluded with a dramatic death dive into Saturn in 2017, Spilker returned to Voyager, where she serves as a project scientist today.

"I'm very proud and happy to work on Voyager," she said.

The Voyager team is small, with just eight to 10 people on the flight team, according to Spilker. But they often bring in retired scientists and Voyager team members from decades past who are eager to share their knowledge and connect with the new generation of mission scientists and engineers.

"Voyager is multi-generational," Spilker shared. "We have someone whose parents weren't born when Voyager was launched, and then we just celebrated the 90th birthday of one of the members who retired and came back. He actually helped to build and program the computers on Voyager."

Looking to the future, the team is pressing on full speed ahead to continue science with Voyager. Another big milestone is just ahead, when the mission turns 50 this upcoming year. And Spilker is optimistic that this will not be the end.

"I see the 50th anniversary as just a milestone," Spilker said. "The next milestone, and then we'll just keep on going."

As Voyager 1 hits one light-day from Earth, you might wonder whenVoyager 2 will hit the same milestone. Since Voyager 2 is on a slower trajectory,it won't reach one light-day from Earth until 2035, nearly a decade into the future. The Voyagers are both hardy and tough, so it's not crazy to think the probe may still be alive when it crosses that threshold.

#807. Sarah Michelle Gellar Reveals Surprising Freddie Prinze Jr. Connection

Sarah Michelle Gellar told E! News that through Ancestry, with whom she partnered for its Gathering the Good initiative, she and Freddie Prinze Jr. learned they have a mutual connection to The Bronx.

Now this is a revelation to wig out over.

Sarah Michelle Gellar and Freddie Prinze Jr.’s paths didn’t officially cross until the late ‘90s on I Know What You Did Last Summer, but as they recently learned they had more in common than they realized. Specifically, a shared family experience that traces back decades before they graced the screen.

“We always joke that the closest connection I had to my husband's side of the family,” Gellar told E! News in an exclusive interview, “was that for a small time I went to the same high school that my husband's dad went to, and that was like sort of our one thing.”

After all, though Gellar—mom to Charlotte, 17, and Rocky, 14, with Prinze—is a native New Yorker, her husband was born in Los Angeles and grew up in New Mexico. (His dad Freddie Prinze, however, hailed from New York.)

She continued, “Then through Ancestry, we found out that our grandparents lived less than two miles away from each other in the Bronx at one point, which they could have potentially known each other. That's kind of crazy.”

For the Buffy the Vampire Slayer star, who teamed up with Ancestry for its Gathering the Good initiative, it was an opportunity to explore her own family’s legacy while also looking at the spirit of giving through history. So, tracing how her loved ones made the journey to America in the 1890s at the same time philanthropist Lena Sittig space was creating what is now considered to be the modern toy drive, really hit home how interconnected the mission is.

“I learned that my grandmother was coming over on a ship at 16 years old, right when Lena was having her idea for this,” she shared. “It’s kind of crazy how the world intertwines, and it just reminds you that you're just such a small part of such a bigger picture.”

It’s especially poignant as diving back into her roots has not always been a focal point for Gellar.

“It's funny, I didn't really spend that much time thinking about my history and my ancestry because I try so hard to live in the moment,” she explained. “And when Ancestry came to me and talked about what they wanted to do, I thought, ‘What a great idea to be able to learn acts of kindness, acts of goodness that your family may have been a part of that you never knew.’”

As the Cruel Intentions alum knows, ‘tis the season to pay it forward. “The holiday season gets so dramatic—presents and all that,” she noted. “And I always look for what are the things that you could give someone that are really meaningful.”

So, the 49-year-old posited, “What's more meaningful than learning about where you came from and your family and things you may not have known?”

To Gellar, it all comes back to Lena Sittig and her Brooklyn Christmas Tree Society, and how her idea is sparking change so many generations later. In fact, the Ringer actress teamed up with Ancestry to fulfill Christmas lists for Children’s Aid.

“So often, I think we think, ‘Well, I'm one person. What can I do?’ And then you see something like that, and you realize, oh wow, one person can do a lot,” she told E!. “But then to take it that step further, and maybe there's people in her family had no idea they were related to her.”

“Can you imagine going back in your history and finding out that one person in your family was responsible for millions of children's gifts all over the world because they had this idea?” Gellar added. “I think it's really special.”

And it’s an experience Gellar wants to send far and wide, teasing what many of her loved ones—not to mention anyone looking to explore the impact their family has made on others—may be getting under the tree this year.

“There's something for me about the how tangible it was,” she admitted. “I saw signatures, I saw writing. it makes it seem just much more real to you than just getting an email that says, ‘You know you came from here’ like, seeing their actual signatures at Ellis Island. It's also something too, growing up in New York City, you forget about it. But this is the gateway.”

And for Gellar it also ended up being a sweet gateway into a piece of history she and Prinze didn’t realize they shared. For a deeper history of the longtime couple’s life together, keep reading…

#805. India's SatLeo Labs wants to build a 'thermometer for Earth' in space

Thermal satellites from an Indian startup aim to spot urban heat, crop stress and wildfires from orbit.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

AHMEDABAD, India — As climate disasters grow more frequent and severe, a young Indian space-tech startup is betting it can help the world act sooner by reading Earth's temperature from orbit in near-real time.

SatLeo Labs, based here in western India, is building what it calls a "thermometer for Earth" in space. It plans to achieve its roadmap to deliver frequent, near-real-time thermal data through Pyro, a planned constellation of 15 microsatellites that will circle the planet in low Earth orbit by early 2030, if all goes to plan. Equipped with thermal sensors and onboard artificial intelligence, the satellites will measure the heat radiating from Earth's surface at a resolution finer than 10 meters (33 feet), which is sharp enough to map heat variations down to street level, the company says.

"It's going to be that precise," SatLeo Labs co-founder Urmil Bakhai told Space.com in a recent interview.

That level of detail, he said, helps distinguish temperatures across a single city and pinpoint urban hot spots, allowing governments and policymakers to plan targeted interventions and more heat-resilient city designs.

The company is also targeting agriculture, and for good reason: Research suggests that thermal data can directly reveal water stress on crops days before leaves wilt, discolor or show other visible damage, unlike visible-light satellite imagery. Other uses the company is eyeing include spotting forest fires early, tracking industrial emissions and, on the defense side, detecting sudden temperature spikes from missile launches.

Down the road, the team also envisions hyper-local uses. Near the top of its list are live heat maps built into navigation apps that could help gig-economy workers in India. These folks, who often ride motorcycles, could use the data to pick cooler routes during heat waves, said Bakhai.

"We are in space, but we're solving problems on Earth," said Shravan Bhati, SatLeo's co-founder and CEO.

First, however, the company has to prove that its homegrown hardware works in space. On Oct. 1, SatLeo launched its first technology demonstrator, TAPAS-1, aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket as part of the Transporter-18 rideshare mission. Short for "Thermal Access Platform for Analytics & Solutions," TAPAS-1 is India's first commercial thermal payload in orbit and the first of SatLeo's three planned test payloads meant to validate its technology.

Once complete, the 15-satellite Pyro fleet will scan all of the world's land surface at least twice a day, Bakhai said. Successful deployment of that fleet would make SatLeo one of just a few private thermal-imaging operators across the world, such as SatVu in the U.K. and OroraTech in Germany.

The company has raised roughly $6 million since it was founded in 2023, and it holds letters of intent worth $54 million from prospective customers, Bakhai said.

SatLeo grew out of a government project that used satellite data for farming insights. Its founders found existing thermal data, such as from the U.S. government's Landsat satellites or Earth-observing craft operated by the San Francisco company Planet Labs, too coarse for India's fragmented farmlands, Bakhai said. When field teams and drones couldn't fill the gap at scale, "we realized space is the only solution," he said.

SatLeo's orbital ambitions take shape on the ground, inside a light-blocked cleanroom at the company's headquarters here in Ahmedabad. When Space.com visited in late October, about three weeks after TAPAS-1 launched, a handful of engineers in cleanroom coats were already fine-tuning its successor, TAPAS-2.

The payload itself sat perched on a solitary, nondescript table with a thick, hole-filled steel top meant to dampen vibrations from footsteps, traffic and the like. The room's only window was covered by a thick black blind to seal out stray light, a necessity for calibrating sensors meant to track the planet's thermal pulse from a few hundred kilometers up.

Despite its small size, the payload is built to collect enormous amounts of data. How much detail a payload can capture "all depends upon the architecture of the detector," said SatLeo co-founder Ranendu Ghosh, a former scientist at the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO).

The design captures two infrared bands, mid-wave and long-wave, on the same payload. The company says this lets a single design serve both civilian and defense uses: long-wave suits applications like agriculture, while the hotter signatures of fires or missile launches show up better in mid-wave.

TAPAS-1 took just six months to build, and TAPAS-2 is on a similar timeline: It's expected to be ready by February 2027, according to the team.

Access to government test facilities explains much of that speed, Bhati said. Rather than buy capital-intensive equipment, such as a thermal vacuum chamber that mimics conditions in space, the company calibrates its payloads at facilities run by IN-SPACe, the government agency that supports private space firms, and ISRO's Space Applications Centre, both in Ahmedabad.

A small group of former ISRO scientists, about eight among a staff of around 40, also mentored the younger workforce and "really made this journey a little faster for us," Bakhai said.

Ghosh, who spent more than two decades at ISRO, said the nature of a private company helps, too. "When I was in ISRO, I saw people delivering this kind of a payload," he said. "I never saw it delivered in less than a year."

He credited the SatLeo team's "zeal to deliver in time," along with fewer administrative challenges than at ISRO, which he described as an organization where "you cannot bypass the hierarchy."

The harder constraint, the founders said, is not building satellites but finding rockets to carry them to space. TAPAS-1's launch slipped from a planned February liftoff to October for lack of a ride, Bakhai said.

SpaceX is reportedly not accepting new bookings until at least 2029. In addition, Skyroot Aerospace, which in July became the first Indian company to reach orbit, is still flying development missions meant to validate its Vikram-1 rocket before it begins full-scale commercial operations.

"There is a challenge right now in terms of availability of launch vehicles," Bakhai said. Once additional Indian rockets, such as those built by Skyroot and Agnikul, are flying regularly, "things will be much easier."

SatLeo is among more than 400 space startups that have emerged in India since the government opened the sector to private participation in 2020. Driven by this new wave of private enterprise, the country's space economy — currently valued at about $9 billion — is estimated to reach $40 billion over the next decade.

Asked what advice they would give newcomers entering the growing industry, SatLeo's three co-founders offered a unified message for success: start with the problem, then decide what to build.

"If you're solving a problem," Bhati said, "then people will bet on you."

Sharmila Kuthunur is an independent space journalist based in Bengaluru, India. Her work has also appeared in Scientific American, Science, Astronomy and Live Science, among other publications. She holds a master's degree in journalism from Northeastern University in Boston.

#804. Sleuth finds ‘impossible proteins’ in hundreds of research papers

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Some studies show the expression of proteins such as caspase-3 (pictured), in cell lines that should not be able to produce them. Credit: Dr Mark J. Winter/Science Photo Library

A scientific sleuth has identified more than 220 research papers that describe impossible patterns of protein expression in genetically altered cell lines. In these studies, particular proteins show up in imaging experiments, even though the cells do not have the gene necessary to make them.

Journals are now taking action to clean up the literature by retracting or correcting the work, and researchers warn that there are probably many more affected studies.

“This problem will not go away,” says Thierry Soussi, a cancer geneticist at Uppsala University in Sweden, who notes that there are several other examples of the issue in now-retracted papers that were not included in the sleuth’s analysis. “This is only the tip of a gigantic iceberg.”

Cell lines are groups of cells derived from a single origin cell and cultured for use in experiments. Some cancer cell lines have been genetically modified with mutations and deletions — often to remove genes that usually control cell division. This means that the cultures continually divide and grow, giving researchers the chance to study tumour progression and test potential treatments.

The MCF-7 cell line is one of these. It lacks the gene for caspase-3 protein, which is involved in cell death. In 2009, researchers warned1 that some studies that report working with MCF-7 have mysteriously observed caspase-3 expression in western blots, an imaging technique that identifies proteins based on their molecular weight.

Sleuth identifies dozens of studies that used the wrong antibody

Sleuth identifies dozens of studies that used the wrong antibody

In the most recent analysis, published as a preprint on 21 October to the data repository Zenodo2, Sholto David, a sleuth based in Arbroath, UK, finds that this problem persists and extends to other cell lines.

David compiled a list of 20 commonly used cell lines with genetic mutations or deletions that leave cells unable to express specific proteins. He then scoured the literature using Google text and image searches to identify examples of western-blot images that unexpectedly identify these proteins. He also searched a collection of 140,000 articles that he had previously downloaded and screened for image-integrity issues and other problems, most of which were biomedicine papers.

He found 230 reports of phantom proteins across 221 papers published since 2004. The most common errors were observations of caspase-3 expression in the MCF-7 cell line, affecting 49 papers; expression of the cell-death protein BAX in the Jurkat cell line in 47 papers; and expression of the signalling protein STAT3 in the PC-3 cell line in 35 papers.

David suggests several explanations for these impossible protein-expression patterns. They might be the result of honest errors: researchers could have misidentified the cell lines or contaminated them with others. Or the antibodies used to identify proteins in the western-blot experiments could have been non-specific and bound to another protein with the same molecular weight. In fact, David says that he stumbled across the anomalous proteins while working on a project that flagged hundreds of studies that used the wrong antibodies in experiments.

Another possibility is that some of the papers are the product of papermills, companies that fabricate and sell scientific manuscripts. David says that some papers in the cache contain the hallmarks of being produced by such outfits, including duplicated images or text templates that are similar to other papers. The proportion of the papers that fall into this category is not clear, he says.

Nature has contacted several authors of papers containing anomalies to ask for comment, but none responded.

#803. Miss Universe Vietnam 2026 Stripped of Title After 2 Months

After Miss Universe Vietnam crowned Nguyen Quynh Anh its 2026 winner on Oct. 2, the beauty queen's title was revoked following a controversy that began with a leaked group chat.

Nguyen Quynh Anh's reign as Miss Universe Vietnam has officially come to an end.

The beauty queen was initially suspended in October when private messages speaking negatively about other pageant participants became public, and now the organizers have revoked her title due to Nguyen's conduct while under suspension.

The issues occurred while Nguyen was barred from performing in all "artistic performance activities" related to Miss Universe for six months, the show’s organizers, Five6 Entertainment, announced in a Nov. 18 statement, according to Tuoi Tre News.

In addition to being suspended from events for the group text—which included runner-up Trinh My Anh—containing derogatory remarks about past winners, fellow contestants and judges, the model was ordered to pay a fine, the outlet said.

However, when the influencer attended a community event while banned from representing the pageant, the production company, per Tuoi Tre News, said her appearance caused issues that "affected the image of Miss Universe Vietnam and its organizers."

In addition to promoting her title while suspended, the organizers stated that the 27-year-old delayed signing her management contract in order to prioritize a "mental health condition" amid the transitional period. Still, the team said they learned Nguyen signed an exclusive contract with a competitor management agency and "continued accepting performance engagements and attending events without reaching an agreement with Five6."

In response to the initial backlash, the competition's runner-up, Trinh, apologized on Instagram. Meanwhile, Nguyen released an Oct. 13 statement transcribed by the outlet where she apologized "to the women concerned and everyone affected by this incident, especially the audience."

"I understand that holding a beauty queen title does not make me incapable of making mistakes," her statement continued. "However, the title requires me to be more mindful and careful about my words, conduct and responsibilities, even in seemingly minor matters."

E! News has reached out to Nguyen Quynh Anh regarding the recent conduct allegations but has not yet heard back.

The release noted that her title was formally revoked after reviewing the conditions of holding the crown, the outlet said.

And given the unexpected exit, Vietnam will not send a competitor to the global Miss Universe finale on Nov. 24 in Puerto Rico.

#802. Fernandez dropped, Anderson scores - Man City's £327m midfield dilemma

Man City drop points to Fulham despite superb Anderson volley

There may have been some eyebrows raised before kick-off when Manchester City manager Enzo Maresca decided to drop club record signing Enzo Fernandez to the bench against Fulham.

Fernandez's lengthy excursions back home to Argentina for their two fixtures during the international break may have been a factor in Maresca's thinking when selecting his starting XI for this game.

If it was, the Italian refrained from giving that as a reason. "I just think for this game it's better having Ayyoub Bouaddi in there," he told TNT Sports shortly before kick-off.

Even so, the move was a significant one as his side were in desperate need of victory after suffering three straight Premier League defeats. That winless streak extended to four after being held to a 1-1 draw.

Maresca had an opportunity to fix the issues in his set-up during the two-week break and admitted on Friday he was searching for "more balance" in the "defensive line, midfield and up front".

The pairing of the steady Bouaddi and all-action Elliot Anderson in the centre of the park was the crucial call, and it may have given Maresca some idea as to how to approach the forthcoming run of games.

"Ayyoub with Elliot were both really good," said Maresca. "Today we used Elliot a bit more attacking midfielder, he arrived inside the box and scored a fantastic goal, he had three or four moments around the box where he was really dangerous.

"It is another solution for us. In this moment, we are trying to know each other more as players and also to find the right solution."

Anderson rescues Man City point against Fulham

Anderson steps up, Berge impresses - player ratings for Man City v Fulham

Elliot Anderson and Ayyoub Bouaddi both joined Manchester City in the summer

Loud jeers greeted the full-time whistle at Etihad Stadium, a culmination of the feeling that was brewing from the home supporters throughout the game.

There was a nervous tension from the beginning, which seemed to seep on to the players on the pitch.

City displayed a flat first-half performance in which they fell behind courtesy of Rodrigo Muniz's superb curling effort, and they needed a stunning second-half volley from Anderson to rescue a point.

The England international is restricted to sitting in front of the back four when Fernandez is in the side, but has the licence to roam when Bouaddi is deployed beside him.

Aside from scoring a spectacular first Premier League goal for City, Anderson created a match-high three chances and had a 100% success rate from 16 passes in the final third of the pitch.

He also had more touches in the opposition box (7), contested more duels than any other player (17) and no-one else managed to win possession back more times than him.

After dragging his side level, another marauding run into the box was snuffed out by the visiting defenders before Rayan Cherki was brought on, which meant Anderson had to retreat back down the pitch.

Maresca needed to change things in order to apply some fresh impetus in the attacking third, but the substitution of Cherki for Phil Foden seemed to limit Anderson's capabilities.

"It's not a good result, especially off the back of three losses," former City goalkeeper Joe Hart told BBC Sport. "There was some good stuff in there.

"It felt like Elliot Anderson was going to take the game by the scruff of the neck but then Cherki came on and took his position. So he [Anderson] didn't have as much of an impact on the game.

"I understood the change - when the lines are deep, there were chances of Cherki unlocking Fulham, but they just defended so well and they also offered a threat on the break."

Leno hopes Hart has his back on MOTD tonight...

City overhauled their midfield to the tune of Â£327m with the signings of trio Fernandez, Anderson and Bouaddi.

The Â£125m club record acquisition Fernandez had made the 14,000-mile round-trip from Manchester to Buenos Aires for Argentina's friendlies against Uruguay and Costa Rica.

The trip allowed him to take the opportunity to pay a visit to boyhood club River Plate, but it is at his current club where there are question marks as to how he fits into the side.

Bouaddi's presence provides more insurance in front of the defence and the 19-year-old Moroccan has the ability to keep the ball ticking.

It means Anderson can play his natural game - but where, then, does Fernandez fit in?

The number 10 position tends to be occupied by either Cherki or Foden, while Maresca pointed out in his pre-match news conference that City "won games with Enzo and lost games with Enzo".

But the manager clearly has to work out how to get the best out of Fernandez, who was given the final five minutes against Fulham in place of Bouaddi.

"There is no point in having a brilliant squad like Manchester City if you are not going to take that into account," said Hart.

"It's very much understandable, if you're going to have a squad and you trust everyone - if someone's done the travelling, he has done the game time, you have got to expect to not use him as much."

City host Napoli in the Champions League on Tuesday followed by a huge trip to Arsenal next Sunday, knowing they could head to the Emirates eight points behind the champions.

Maresca added: "For sure we don't like these kind of moments in terms of four games in a row without a win

"We also know that, unfortunately, it is normal or part of the path, you go through these kind of moments. It is important that we find a way to keep clean sheets that sometimes you need to win games 1-0 for a small difference."

Mikel Arteta's men know all about that and City now need to take a leaf out of their book.

#801. Tristan Thompson Reveals His “Home Run” Investment in Anthropic AI

NBA player Tristan Thompson—who shares kids True, 8, and Tatum, 4, with Khloe Kardashian—said he invested in Anthropic AI years ago and is seeing the rewards after it raised over $81 billion in IPO.

Tristan Thompson has made nothing but net gains.

At least, that’s true when it comes to his early investment in Anthropic AI, the artificial intelligence company that saw major financial wins this week when it went public and sold $81.3 billion worth of stock shares, according to CNBC.

Noting he's “happy" about the company's recent successes, Thompson told Yahoo Finance that he got involved in the tech brand over two years ago while visiting San Francisco as part of his NBA schedule when he was playing for the Cleveland Cavaliers.

Thompson—who shares kids True, 8, and Tatum, 4, with ex Khloe Kardashian—met up with Sriram Krishnan, now a Senior White House Policy Advisor on Artificial Intelligence, who he described as a "great buddy of mine."

"The only friend that I had in SF during those Finals runs that was picking the Cavaliers to win, he opened up these doors," Thompson recalled in the interview published Nov. 19. "Going to dinners and and meeting people. I think SF is one of those towns where a lot of great founders and early startups, they want to come together and build this ecosystem."

"And I said, 'You know what? Let me insert myself in,'" the 35-year-old said. "I'm the tall guy walking in. I'm probably about 10 inches taller than everyone else, and [say], 'Tell me what you're working on.'"

Now, years after becoming an investor, Thompson explained how thrilled they were last month when Anthropic announced it had filed a proposed stock plan with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission.

"We're in a group chat and everyone's just talking about what they're going to do to celebrate," Thompson shared. "I said, 'Guys, the one thing we have to do is do a dinner. We got to break bread again.'"

As he put it, "Cheers to getting it right this time."

Because, as the Miami Heat player admitted, his ventures don't always pay off like Anthropic did, breaking records with its initial public offering (CNBC reported it had a fully diluted market cap of about $1.8 trillion on Nov. 19).

"Listen, out of 10 companies you invest in, you're lucky if two make it to the finish line and get the home run," Thompson explained. "But what I tell people is those two that make it to the finish line and win that championship in their eyes for what the company's trying to do, it will make up for all the capital that you invested in."

As for whether he plans to cash out of Anthropic? Not so fast—he sees himself as a long-term shareholder.

"I'm extremely bullish," Thompson added. "Their alignment with government definitely makes you feel very bullish about it. It's almost like investing in Google during the dot com era."

For more stars getting candid on their finances and paychecks, read on.

(E! and CNBC are both part of Versant Media.)

The Jackass star reflected on the "comical" amount of money he was paid for doing death-defying stunts on the MTV series' first season in 2000.

"When it was all said and done, after taxes, I was paid less than $1,500 for the entire first season of Jackass," the daredevil told Playboy in June 2026. "Before the show came out, my sister kicked me out of the house. I was broke, unemployed, and homeless, and a star on this big MTV show."

Oscar winner Jennifer Lawrence was paid $25 million to star in Adam McKay’s ensemble disaster comedy Don’t Look Up. But her costar and fellow Oscar winner Leonardo DiCaprio got $30 million.

“Look, Leo brings in more box office than I do,” Lawrence told Vanity Fair for its’ December 2020/January 2021 issue. “I’m extremely fortunate and happy with my deal. But in other situations, what I have seen—and I’m sure other women in the workforce have seen as well—is that it’s extremely uncomfortable to inquire about equal pay. And if you do question something that appears unequal, you’re told it’s not gender disparity but they can’t tell you what exactly it is.”

Her sanguine attitude was hard-fought: When the disparity between Lawrence’s compensation and that of her male costars for 2013’s American Hustle was revealed in the 2014 Sony email hack, it prompted an industry-wide conversation about the gender pay gap in Hollywood.

"I'm so fortunate to have my job. My problem is not money," Lawrence told the U.K.’s Channel 4 News in 2017. "I wasn't upset that I only got this many millions for a movie. That's ridiculous. I was angry about the unfairness and inequality."

The *NSYNC alum revealed that he and his fellow bandmates JC Chasez, Joey Fatone, Chris Kirkpatrick and Justin Timberlake didn't make much money during their years with the group.

“We had a per diem: $35 a day,” he revealed on The Zach Sang Show in 2026. “Our first check was a $10,000 check after years of No. 1 albums, sellout tours. I don’t know how many millions they made off of merchandise because merchandise was insane.”

“And then they finally gave us a check for $10,000,” he recalled. “You’re like, ‘Oh, thanks.’ We should be grateful for that, been working for free for two, three years now.”

Less comparable to DiCaprio’s salary: The $60,000 “before commissions and taxes” that Jonah Hill was paid for 2013’s The Wolf of Wall Street, while the titular wolf made $10 million.

“They gave me the lowest amount of money possible,” Hill recalled on The Howard Stern Show in 2014. But it was the chance to appear in a Martin Scorsese movie, so the Moneyball alum wanted to get the deal done before anyone could change their mind.

“I would sell my house and give him all my money to work for [Scorsese],” explained Hill, who earned his second Best Supporting Actor nomination for his turn as a squirrelly substance-abusing stockbroker. “This isn't what you make money for. You do 22 Jump Street or you do other things, and you can pay your rent. I would have done anything in the world. I would do it again in a second. This isn't about money. You should do things that you care about."

According to Dylan Sprouse, his residuals from filming The Suite Life of Zack & Cody with twin brother Cole Sprouse is anything but suite.

"The only residual check I've ever received for The Suite Life at all was a crossover episode with Hannah Montana for five cents," the Disney Channel alum shared during a 2026 episode of his Wildmen podcast. "In a time where residuals would have been great, not a single paycheck for being arguably one of the most popular shows on television."

While there's no cash prize for nabbing Dancing With the Stars' mirrorball trophy, “whoever makes it to the finale, you all get paid up until then," Jenna Johnson, who won season 33 with partner Joey Graziadei, shared. "And you do get a nice bonus.”

"If you win," Johnson, who noted pro contracts are dependent on seniority, continued. "it’s not like you get a million dollars. You’re just getting a cute trophy together.” As for those who say farewell to the ballroom early, well, as she explained, "You’re guaranteed until a certain amount of weeks.” According to multiple reports, dancer salaries start at around $1,200 to $1,600 an episode, which can increase to up to of $100,000 per season. (ABC has not confirmed these reports.) On the flip side, celebrities receive a starting salary of $125,000. As they cha-cha further into the competition, stars  receive additional bonuses with the semifinalists and finalists getting paid up to $50,000 extra.

The actress seemingly confirmed that the Friends cast—including Jennifer Aniston, Courtney Cox,David Schwimmer and Matt LeBlanc—get $20 million in residuals per year from the show re-airing, quipping to The Times in April 2026 that if she had to guess why, it's “Because Phoebe Buffay was so great?"

But in actuality, she praised the talents of her costars for their performances.

“I felt I did OK, but Jennifer and Courteney? Amazing,” she raved. “David and Matt? They had me laughing so hard. And then Matthew [Perry]—he was just beyond us all.”

To hear Joe Giudice tell it, his and ex-wife Teresa Giudice's salary for season one of The Real Housewives of New Jersey was nothing to flip over. "We got paid nothing the first season," he detailed on daughter Gia Giudice's Casual Chaos podcast in August 2025. "I'll even say, it was like $25,000. It was ridiculous. But, whatever."

And the ingredientses they put into that initial fame-making season weren't cheap. "I think the first year we had that big party in my great room," the father of four reflected. "I think that show cost me $150,000 the first year."

Oprah Winfrey happily accepted only a little bit of green to star in 1985’s The Color Purple.

“They were only offering $35,000 to be in this film, and it is the best $35,000 I ever earned,” the billionaire media mogul told Essence in 2023. “It changed everything and taught me so much.”

The actress revealed that she made about $20,000 per episode of Two and a Half Men with a 5 percent raise each season, making about $43,000 for one episode in the final season.

When she scored the role of late Tejana singer Selena Quintanilla in the 1997 biopic Selena, Jennifer Lopez became the first Latina actress to earn $1 million for a film.

“I was too young and didn’t know what the hell was going on,” Lopez told Variety in 2019, reflecting on her breakout movie. “It was great they offered me a million dollars. I feel like everyone was making a statement.”

And it paved the way for her to make hundreds of millions more, though sometimes her participation doesn’t cost a thing.

“I do things because I love them,” Lopez explained to GQ in 2019. “I didn't get paid a whole bunch of money for Hustlers. I did it for free and produced it. I bank on myself, you know? Like Jenny From the Block—I do what I love."

Adrien Brody didn’t do The Brutalist for the money. Rather, he took on the role of a Hungarian architect suffering for his art in post-WWII America for $250,000 and won his second Oscar for Best Actor.

“I need a studio movie now, because I’ve poured it all into this,” Brody quipped to Variety, referring to the “barn that looks like a castle” he’s renovating in upstate New York.

“Do you guys know what they pay us?” Pete Davidson cracked to New York magazine when asked ahead of Saturday Night Live's 50th anniversary special how he spent his money when he was first hired at the age of 20 in 2014. “It’s like three grand an episode, so I think I got dinner.”

Interestingly, the salaries have remained proportional for SNL newcomers, with season one stars John Belushi, Jane Curtin, Gilda Radner, Dan Aykroyd and Chevy Chase reportedly earning $750 an episode back in 1975. Which was roughly equivalent to $3,300 in 2014, according to the Consumer Price Index Inflation calculator. (Though the $750 of 1975 is $4,428 in 2025.)

While Kenan Thompson makes a lot more than $3,000 per episode of SNL now that he’s in his record 22nd season, the former Nickelodeon star had to start somewhere.

“That first commercial when they paid me, it was $800,” the All That alum revealed in Demi Lovato‘s 2024 documentary Child Star. “I was 12 so that may as well have been a million dollars."

It turns out Gilmore Girls’ status as a beloved rewatchable classic is literally priceless.

“There really are no residuals on Netflix,” Lauren Graham, who played Lorelai Gilmore for seven seasons and then reprised the role for 2016’s Gilmore Girls: A Year in the Life, said on Jimmy Kimmel Live in March 2025. “But I’ve been paid in love and appreciation.”

Feeling not so appreciated, Tommy Dorfman got specific about her 13 Reasons Why paycheck during the 2023 SAG-AFTRA strike—which was prompted in part (as was the WGA strike) by streamers like Netflix not making it a practice to pay additional compensation to cast and crew once a show had become a big hit.

"my earnings for the entire first season of 13 reasons why were $29,953.24 prior to agency and manager fees (20%) and taxes," Dorfman wrote on Threads July 24. "8 episodes over six months." She continued, “i did all of the promo and had KEY ART for this show, flew round trip from NYC to SF to shoot for every episode, was kept for days without pay/working. i barely qualified for insurance."

And, Dorfman added, “within the first 28 days of release, the show's season 1 garnered a total of 476 million view hours. this is why we strike."

Without naming names or numbers, Dax Shepard told fellow Parenthood alum Lauren Graham when she appeared on his podcast that he knew he made “among the lowest of all the actors” on their NBC drama, which ran for six seasons.

But, the Armchair Expert host stressed that he did not mind.

“Every job I had ever had in my life prior to Parenthood, I made a point to find out what everyone was making,” he said. “I'd always figure it out—either a conversation where I get it out of them or I backchannel through an agent."

So he made a point to purposely not seek out such info about his Parenthood family, which helped with enjoying the experience even when he did get an inkling of where he was on the pay pyramid.

“I got a dollar for writing the script,” George Clooney told the Los Angeles Times in 2005 about the financial strings he pulled to get his film Good Night, and Good Luck made. “I had to endorse my check for directing and turn in my acting salary. [Actor, cowriter and coproducer Grant Heslov] and I each made a buck for doing it.”

His labor of love about CBS News journalist Edward R. Murrow speaking truth to power in the 1950s had legs, though: Making his Broadway debut, Clooney wrapped his months-long stint playing Murrow in a stage adaptation of the film  in June 2025. And with the play having grossed a Broadway record (for a nonmusical) $3.3 million during a preview week before it officially opened April 3, he made a lot more than $1.

For his chilling turn as Patrick Bateman in 2000’s American Psycho, Christian Bale was paid “the absolute minimum they were legally allowed to pay me” because no one in the production really wanted to hire him except director Mary Harron, the Welsh actor told GQ in 2022.

He made so little, Bale shared, that he remembered “sitting in the makeup trailer and the makeup artists were laughing at me because I was getting paid less than any of them.”

No, the Game of Thrones cast didn't get paid $300,000 per episode, according to Emilia Clarke.

“We didn’t earn that much," she told Variety in 2026. "Can you imagine? I’d have been driving a couple of Porsches!"

However, the actress—who played Daenerys Targaryen for eight seasons between 2011 and 2019—noted that the money she made throughout the HBO show did provide her with enough financial security to pay off her parents’ mortgage.

His uncle may have been Rico, but Jon Heder confirmed in 2010 that he was “initially” only paid $1,000 for Napoleon Dynamite.

After the irreverent comedy became a sleeper hit, he was able to renegotiate for a piece of the profits, telling the New Zealand Herald, “They went a little bit higher.”

Djimon Hounsou said he’s “definitely underpaid” in Hollywood despite his prestigious list of credits, including Amistad and Blood Diamond.

"I've been in this business and making films now over two decades," the Beninese actor told CNN’s Larry Madowo in January 2025. "And still—with two Oscar nominations and been in many big blockbuster films—and yet I’m still struggling financially to make a living."

Rebel Wilson detailed in her 2024 memoir Rebel Rising that she was paid $3,500 to do Bridesmaids, “a fee that I then had to pay directly to the Screen Actors Guild to join the union. So really, I got paid nothing.”

Still, she wrote, the experience was “everything!”

And the Australian actress’ star rose ever a-ca higher, with her fee going from the SAG minimum scale of $65,000 for 2012’s Pitch Perfect to $10 million for 2017’s Pitch Perfect 3. Wilson wrote that she raked in $20 million total for the threequel, Isn’t It Romantic and The Hustle, though—reality alert—she “lost almost 50 percent to taxes, 10 percent to agents and 5 percent” to her lawyer. But even after those obligations and paying her publicist, business manager and assistant, Wilson “netted what to me was an absolute fortune.”

In late 2017, Ellen Pompeo negotiated a new Grey’s Anatomy contract for $575,000 per episode, a seven-figure signing bonus and two full backend equity points worth an estimated $6 million to $7 million.

“I’m 48 now, so I’ve finally gotten to the place where I’m OK asking for what I deserve, which is something that comes only with age,” Pompeo told The Hollywood Reporter in 2018. “Because I’m not the most ‘relevant’ actress out there. I know that’s the industry perception because I’ve been this character for 14 years. But the truth is, anybody can be good on a show season one and two. Can you be good 14 years later? Now, that’s a f--kin’ skill.”

Reflecting more recently on how she always made less than costar Patrick Dempsey, even though she was the Grey in question, Pompeo said she didn’t begrudge him his money.

But, she said on a March 2025 episode of Call Her Daddy, “Just being that I was the namesake of the show, I deserved the same and that was harder to get. I wasn't salty about him getting what he got. I was salty that they didn't value me as much as they valued him and they never will.”

Jamie Lee Curtis recalled getting paid $2,000 a week—so $8,000 in total—for 1978’s Halloween, her movie debut. “I mean,” she told Rotten Tomatoes in 2018, “nobody got paid, anything.”

Yet while the scream queen earned four figures, director John Carpenter’s friend Nick Castle felt like a king making $25 per day to share the role of Michael Myers. (It’s Anthony Moran whose face you see when the killer’s mask comes off for a freaky second, and editor Tommy Lee Wallace also logged screentime as Michael.)

“That was a lot at the time!” Castle, who attended film school at USC with Carpenter, told Vanity Fair in 2018. “You have to remember: My interest in doing the film was being on set, so I could demystify the experience of filmmaking and directing. I expected to hang around the set for no money. But hey, $25 per day, and all I had to do was wear a rubber mask.”

Taraji P. Henson earned a Best Supporting Actress Oscar nomination for 2008’s The Curious Case of Benjamin Button, but years later she was still fired up by the $150,000 she accepted to be in the movie—after producers rejected the $500,000 quote she brought to the table.

As for the film’s leads Brad Pitt and Cate Blanchett, “You don’t hear a lot of $20 million quotes anymore, but at this time that was happening,” Henson said on the Ladies First With Laura Brown podcast in 2021. “And rightfully so—I’m not saying they shouldn’t have paid Cate and Brad what they deserved.”

But, she continued, “I’m bringing a certain amount to the seat too and I felt like what I was asking at that time in my career was fair, was fair to the ticket sales that I would contribute to this big film. Wouldn’t do it.” Henson was “gutted” when they offered $100,000, she recalled. “When it was all said and done I got $150,000, but I had to swallow my pride, baby.”

Breaking it down, “I know people go, ‘$150,000, that’s a lot of money!’” Henson acknowledged. “I don’t ever want people to think that I’m ungrateful because that is not me.” But, she calculated, “Uncle Sam is going to take 50 percent of that, so now you’re left with, what? $75,000. Now before Uncle Sam takes the money, I have to pay my team before taxes, 30 percent. So once Uncle Sam takes his 75, then I got another 30 that’s coming off of that 75, so I may have made $40,000?”

While Blanchett has made plenty of money over the years, it didn’t all come from playing royal elf Galadriel in The Lord of the Rings franchise, though it grossed $2.9 billion at the worldwide box office.

“Are you kidding me? No,” she retorted on Watch What Happens Live in August 2024 when Andy Cohen guessed LOTR was her biggest paycheck. “No one got paid anything to do that movie…I mean, I basically got free sandwiches, and I got to keep my ears.”

They weren’t paid a precious amount, that is. Orlando Bloom, who played elven warrior Legolas, shared on The Howard Stern Show in 2023 that he made $175,000 for the whole trilogy.

#800. Can global leaders put their money where their mouth is on climate?

World leaders warn that geopolitical divisions are distracting from the climate crisis as negotiations focus on clean energy and financing, while Iran calls for compensation for war-related environmental damage.

The slow international response to climate change has placed the world on a path to destruction, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres told heads of state and government during opening statements at this year's COP31 climate conference.

"The ⁠brutal truth is that the climate crisis is outrunning us," he said, as world leaders gathered in the Turkish resort city of Antalya to set the tone for negotiations at the UN climate summit.

A UN reportlast month found ​the world will cross a temperature threshold countries agreed to pursue in order to prevent runaway global heating. At the same time, states like Germany are slipping down the rankings for climate action, according to the annual Climate Change Performance Index published Wednesday by New Climate Institute and Germanwatch.

Nonetheless, Guterres said the world has "the power to make sure the overshoot is a temporary breach."

Negotiators from close to 200 countries are meeting in Turkey at the end of a year characterized by extreme heat waves and a glacier collapse in Nepal that triggered a flood, killing more than 1,400 people and leaving thousands more missing.

At this year's talks, national representatives are discussing climate solutions such as increasing the share of electricity in an effort to move away from fossil fuels.

On Thursday, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, one of the few heads of government from Europe's major economies attending the summit, said that the world's dependence on fossil fuels was at the heart of both the climate crisis and energy security challenges.

"The shift to clean energy is the only route to energy security," he said, endorsing the conference's focus on electrification which he said would lower energy bills, create jobs and protect people from the volatility of fossil fuel markets.

Burnham promised a "new era of British leadership over the next decade," announcing the UK would put climate resilience high on the agenda during its G20 presidency next year.

The US, the world's largest historical emitter of damaging greenhouse gases, is not attending the summit — for the second year in a row after US President Donald Trump withdrew the country from the Paris Agreement in 2025.

Other nations, including big polluters like Germany, France, Italy, Canada and Japan, also opted not to send their top leaders to the talks.

On Wednesday, Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, who is hosting COP31 together with Australia, which is leading negotiations, called on developed nations to take greater responsibility on climate finance.

Financing disagreements center around who should pay for international climate action, whether funding should take the form of grants or loans and how to scale monetary support for developing nations. Many of these countries are among the most vulnerable to the climate crisis but have contributed very little to the emissions causing it.

Erdogan said while previous conferences had resulted in different ideas around financing, they have yet to be turned into action. "We set out to make this an implementation COP," he told leaders.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen addressed remarks that developed nations are not contributing enough to climate finance, saying that the transition away from fossil fuels is in "our common interest."

"Europe is the world's largest provider of climate finance. Last year alone, we contributed more than €32 billion [about $35.5 billion] to support developing countries," she said, adding that Europe will continue to support partners worldwide in tackling climate change.

A recent Carbon Brief analysis found that public funding pledged under the Paris Agreement to help developing countries tackle climate change fell by more than 70% in 2026.

Most multi-year pledges from donor countries expired in 2025. Since then, the US has stepped back from international climate efforts, while several European countries have cut their aid budgets, reported Carbon Brief.

Hilda Heine, president of the Marshall Islands in the Pacific, which face an existential threat from rising sea levels, said the response to overshoot "must be overwhelming" and quickly reversed otherwise "the world we know is over."

"Every fraction of a degree of warming brings more catastrophe," said Heine, adding that more warming makes it more difficult to adapt to living on a hotter planet, brings greater loss and damage from worsening weather extremes and greater financial need.

She called on leaders to triple climate finance by 2035 and make it easier for Small Island Developing States to access the money.

"We are told there is no money, but their spending on war grows; the greatest security threat we face remains underfunded. I appeal to you: Find money for life, not death. Replenish the climate funds," Heine said.

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese spoke of a "solemn responsibility to this and to future generations ​to act," adding that this is the critical decade.

Australia, the world's third-largest fossil fuel exporter, has vowed to promote the views of the "Pacific family" — small Pacific nations in the region such as Tuvalu or Fiji, where pre-COP meetings were held in October.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Albanese said it was crucial that climate cooperation delivered practical results — "unlocking investment in clean energy technologies, accelerating electrification, speeding up action for our oceans, unlocking climate finance for those who need it ​most."

As reasons to speed up electrification von der Leyen pointed to wildfires in Europe and floods in Nepal, as well as droughts stretching from Central America to Sudan, and to the disruption to energy supplies linked to the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz.

"The world is witnessing the cost of continuing with the status quo for our climate and our energy security," she said, adding that the European Union would double down on efforts to become climate neutral.

"Three-quarters ​of humanity live in countries that import fossil fuels, hostage to price shocks they did ​not create and cannot ‌control," UN Secretary-General Guterres said, adding that recent conflicts have made clear a shift to renewable energy would help improve energy security and the cost-of-living crisis.

Von der Leyen also expressed support for COP31's 35-by-35 electrification pledge. The pledge aims to increase electricity's share of final global energy use to 35% by 2035, with von der Leyen saying Europe would be the first "electro-powered" continent.

Heine of the Marshall Islands said electrification must must be strictly tied to renewable energy generation rather than fossil fuels, warning that continued oil, coal and gas extraction was a threat to her country's survival.

Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian said his country wanted compensation for environmental damage caused by US and Israeli strikes, including oil leaks from attacks on tankers. The strikes began in February.

Iran, which is a major fossil fuel producer and has pushed back against strict language on phasing out oil and gas at previous COPs alongside other petrostates, has also struck tankers in the Strait of Hormuz.

Pezeshkian linked the issue to climate finance and said his country expected "responsibility in times of war, to document and assess the environmental damages caused by military aggressions and to develop compensation mechanisms."

Brazil's President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who hosted last year's COP in the Amazonian city of Belem, said the momentum for climate action had dropped off at the start of the year, partly due to the Iran war.

"We started talking more about weapons and tariffs than the survival ‌of future generations," he said.

He also warned that "climate agreements are the favorite targets of reactionary forces at COPs," and urged leaders to work together. Lula promised to protect the Amazon rainforest. "Brazil is back to defend the continuity of a healthy planet," he said.

This article was last updated on November 12 to reflect incoming statements from world leaders.

#799. AC Milan monitoring Man Utd's Fernandes - Sunday's gossip

AC Milan are monitoring Manchester United midfielder Bruno Fernandes, Arsenal pair are yet to start talks on new deals and Trabzonspor renew their interest in Tottenham forward Richarlison.

AC Milan are monitoring the situation of Portugal midfielder Bruno Fernandes, 32, who has yet to agree a contract extension with Manchester United. (Corriere dello Sport - in Italian), external

Manchester United are set to rival Tottenham for Freiburg's Â£50m-rated Croatia striker Igor Matanovic, 23, during the January transfer window. (Goal), external

Norway midfielder Martin Odegaard, 27, and Germany forward Kai Havertz, 27, are about to enter the remaining 18 months of their deals at Arsenal but talks with both about extending their contracts have yet to begin. (Standard), external

Trabzonspor have renewed their interest in Brazil forward Richarlison, 29, with Tottenham looking for a fee of around Â£10m. (The i Paper), external

Juventus are working on a permanent move for Newcastle United loanee Nick Woltemade and may be willing to include Portugal winger Francisco Conceicao, 23, in a swap deal for the 24-year-old Germany forward. (Gazzetta dello Sport via Goal), external

Jack Grealish, 31, is not on Celtic's radar as multiple clubs monitor the former England attacking midfielder, who is out of contract at Manchester City in the summer and currently on loan at Everton. (Football Insider), external

Nottingham Forest's English winger Callum Hudson-Odoi, 26, is a potential January target for Roma. (Teamtalk), external

Uruguay defender Ronald Araujo, 27, says it is too early to think about turning his loan move from Barcelona to Liverpool into a permanent switch. (Athletic - subscription required), external

But Barcelona have given Liverpool the green light to complete a Â£47m deal to buy Araujo. (Mirror), external
