#728. UK court convicts 2 Iranian men of spying on journalists

A London court has found two Iranian citizens guilty of surveilling reporters for a Persian-language television station critical of Iran's government. One was also convicted of planning a violent attack against them.

Two Iranian men were found guilty of spying on dissident journalists in Britain on behalf of Iran's Revolutionary Guard on Thursday.

British counterterrorism police said the case reflected intensifying hostile Iranian activity in the country, an issue that recently made headlines amid the security scare at the RAF Fairford airbase that's a major operational site in Europe for the US Air Force.

The men, both in their 40s, were arrested last year, with Iran repeatedly rejecting the allegations against them.

The Woolwich Crown Court in London convicted one of the Iranian citizens not just of spying on journalists working for the Persian-language dissident TV channel Iran International, but of plotting a violent attack against one or more of them.

The second individual had also faced charges of plotting an attack but was only convicted of spying on the reporters.

One of the convicted defendants said he was acting under duress after his family was threatened, and the other said he did not know that his actions were assisting Iranian intelligence.

A third defendant, a 57-year-old Iranian man, was acquitted of all charges.

The men were accused of engaging in conduct likely to assist the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), Iran's multi-discipline military force that's seen as closer to the country's religious leadership and more influential than its regular armed forces.

The UK formally designated the IRGC as a threat to national security in July, meaning that supporting or assisting the organization can carry penalties of up to 14 years in prison as part of new rules on national security and state threats.

Sentencing in this case is still pending and is scheduled for mid-December.

"This was a calculated operation to spy on those critical of the Iranian regime," said Frank Ferguson, chief prosecutor for the Crown Prosecution Service's special crime and counter-terrorism division.

The two men were accused of visiting addresses linked to their targets, taking photos and videos, and using platforms such as ChatGPT to research them online

"Thankfully, the defendants were stopped before any attack could take place," prosecutor Ferguson said.

Senior ‌National Coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing Vicki Evans said that the IRGC or "middlemen" for Iranian intelligence were directing the plot.

Iran's government had repeatedly denied the allegations, with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi saying he was "disturbed" by the trio's arrests last May.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

There have been four cases targeting the Persian language television channel Iran International since late 2023.

In July, two Romanian men were jailed for stabbing a journalist outside his home in 2024.

A spokesman for the broadcaster's parent company, Volant Media, said in a statement that Thursday's verdicts "don't make the lives of our journalists any safer so long as the Islamic Republic of Iran continues its campaign of death threats and violence against them."

Iran International reported that a British barrister was also one of the targets.

British law enforcement has been warning of an uptick of hostile Iranian activity in recent years, particularly since the US military operations against Tehran began earlier this year.

Most notably, the UK has accused Iran of being behind a suspected plot targeting the RAF Fairford base in September, after which US President Donald Trump withdrew some long-range bombers from the site.

Three men were indicted in the US in relation to that plot this week, while two others currently face charges in the UK.

But beyond this, the head of Britain's MI5 domestic intelligence agency Ken MacCullum said in October that Iran-linked operations had led to more than 50 arrests in the last year. He also said known cases of so-called state threats had more than quadrupled in a decade.

Counter-terrorism police chief Evans said she expected this trend to continue.

France this week also accused Iran of being behind a cyberattack targeting refrigeration units at hundreds of supermarkets in October, although Iran denied any involvement.

European governments are on heightened alert for so-called hybrid warfare tactics, from Russia as well as Iran, amid the geopolitical tensions of recent years. New technologies like low-cost drones and AI are also threatening to make such activities cheaper, harder to trace, and potentially more effective.

#727. A giant icy world hiding beyond Pluto could be our sixth dwarf planet

An enormous icy world discovered beyond Pluto could soon become the sixth officially recognized dwarf planet in our solar system.

The object, temporarily named 2026 ED138, was identified by an astronomer analyzing observations from the Simonyi Survey Telescope at the NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory. Early estimates suggest it ranks among the largest dwarf planet candidates ever found beyond Neptune. If its status is confirmed, it would join the five dwarf planets currently recognized by the International Astronomical Union: Pluto, Ceres, Eris, Haumea and Makemake.

The discovery was announced at a press conference featuring Matthew Holman, a senior astrophysicist at the Harvard & Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics, and Mario Jurić, a University of Washington astronomy professor who leads Rubin's solar system team. Holman made the initial discovery, while Jurić helped gather the additional evidence needed to verify it.

"If confirmed as a dwarf planet, ED138 would join a very small family of worlds," Holman said. "Rubin will image the whole southern sky again and again for 10 years, so any others hiding in the places earlier surveys skipped are now within reach."

"Finding an object this big, roughly 1,000 kilometers across, is something that happens maybe once in a generation," Jurić said. "It's the largest trans-Neptunian object found in about 20 years, and Rubin turned it up while we were still commissioning the telescope."

How Astronomers Discovered the Hidden World

The breakthrough occurred on the evening of October 13, when Holman examined observations gathered by Rubin earlier in 2026. He was using specialized software developed with his colleague Kevin Napier to search for previously unidentified objects moving through the solar system.

The program compares billions of telescope detections, looking for individual points of light that appear in multiple observations and move in ways that suggest they belong to the same object. When the software identified ED138, Holman quickly realized that its apparent brightness and enormous distance pointed to something unusually large.

"My first reaction was one of excited disbelief," Holman said. "Objects like this are very rare, so I immediately started checking whether I or the code had done something wrong."

To check the finding, Jurić examined Rubin's stored observations and located 20 additional detections of ED138, including some captured as early as March 2026. The researchers then searched historical records from other astronomical surveys and identified images of the object dating back to 2016.

Together, these observations allowed the team to reconstruct more than a decade of the distant world's orbital motion, strengthening the evidence that the discovery was genuine.

Could This Be Our Solar System's Sixth Dwarf Planet?

ED138 currently lies approximately 46 astronomical units (au) from the Sun. One astronomical unit represents the average distance separating Earth and the Sun. By comparison, Pluto's average orbital distance is about 40 au.

Because ED138 travels beyond Neptune, astronomers classify it as a trans-Neptunian object (TNO). These distant bodies are valuable to scientists because their physical properties and orbital paths preserve clues about the solar system's distant past.

By examining their sizes, compositions, and movements, researchers can better understand how the solar system developed, how its giant planets shifted positions, and how smaller bodies were redistributed during that process.

However, being a trans-Neptunian object does not automatically make ED138 a dwarf planet. An essential requirement is that the object's gravity must be strong enough to shape it into a nearly round body.

Using measurements of ED138's brightness and distance, along with estimates of how much sunlight its surface reflects, astronomers calculate that it could measure anywhere from 600 to 1,500 kilometers across.

An icy object within that size range would generally be expected to have enough gravity to become round. Nevertheless, scientists will need more observations to establish ED138's actual dimensions and determine whether it qualifies as a dwarf planet.

Why Such a Massive World Remained Undiscovered

One of the most surprising aspects of the discovery is how an object this large managed to escape detection for so long.

ED138 occupies a region of the sky near the plane of the Milky Way, where millions of stars create an exceptionally crowded background. Against that dense field of light, the distant object's faint movement was difficult for earlier telescopes and surveys to distinguish.

Rubin Observatory has an important advantage. Its ability to repeatedly observe the Southern Hemisphere sky, combined with advanced computer algorithms, makes it possible to search enormous quantities of astronomical data for subtle changes in the positions of objects.

By examining millions or even billions of individual light detections, these systems can recognize the movement of small solar system bodies that might otherwise disappear into the surrounding stars. This capability was essential to finding ED138 in such a challenging part of the sky.

Rubin Observatory Could Reveal More Hidden Worlds

The newly identified object adds to a growing collection of solar system discoveries made by Rubin Observatory as it began gathering observations ahead of its ambitious Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST), which officially started in June 2026.

Even before the survey began, the observatory was producing remarkable results. In April, Rubin's solar system researchers reported observations of more than 11,000 previously unknown asteroids, including approximately 380 new trans-Neptunian objects.

The team described that enormous collection of discoveries as "the tip of the iceberg," anticipating that the full survey would uncover many more objects. The identification of ED138 offers an early indication of just how significant those future findings could be.

Rubin's combination of extensive sky coverage, sensitivity, and rapid observations is also changing how astronomers investigate new discoveries. Once an object has been identified, researchers can search older telescope images to find instances when it was photographed but went unrecognized.

"Rubin is giving us an unprecedented capacity to explore the sky through a combination of speed, depth, and precision," Jurić said. "And the discovery is just the beginning: Once we identify a new object, we can search back months, and sometimes even decades, finding it in images where nobody knew to look. This ability to both discover and 'precover' objects is transforming how quickly and accurately we can determine their orbits and understand the distant solar system."

As Rubin continues surveying the southern sky over the next decade, astronomers expect its observations to uncover additional objects that previous searches missed, potentially revealing more large, icy worlds in the outer solar system.

Anyone interested in exploring ED138 can view its location and orbit using Orbitviewer, an interactive web-based application that displays the solar system in three dimensions and allows users to explore its structure in real time.

Operations of the Vera C. Rubin Observatory are funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation and the U.S. Department of Energy's Office of Science.

JAXA has abandoned its plan to rendezvous with the asteroid 1998 KY26, switching to a high-speed flyby of 2015 BM510.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Japan's space agency has decided to switch destinations and objectives for the final act of its Hayabusa2 mission, due to the spacecraft suffering trouble with its ion thrusters.

The veteran Hayabusa2 spacecraft launched back in 2014 to collect material from the asteroid Ryugu. Since delivering the samples to Earth in December 2020 via a reentry capsule, the main spacecraft has been conducting an extended mission of exploration and in July made a super-close flyby of the two-headed asteroid Torifune.

But Hayabusa2's continued adventures are now set for a premature end. The spacecraft was scheduled to rendezvous with, and attempt to land on, the tiny, 36-foot-wide (11 meters) near-Earth asteroid 1998 KY26 in 2031, but trouble with the aging spacecraft's engines has forced a change of plan.

But Hayabusa2's continued adventures are now set for a premature end. The spacecraft was scheduled to rendezvous with, and attempt to land on, the tiny, 36-foot-wide (11 meters) near-Earth asteroid 1998 KY26 in 2031, but trouble with the aging spacecraft's engines has forced a change of plan.

The spacecraft will instead target 2015 BM510, another tiny asteroid. And there will be no landing: Hayabusa2 is scheduled to make a high-speed flyby of the near-Earth object in April 2028.

The decision was announced at a Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) press conference on Tuesday (Nov. 17), a day after a Cabinet Office space policy subcommittee meeting. The final functioning thruster out of Hayabusa2's four ion engines suffered a malfunction in mid-August, according to JAXA officials, while a sensor detected unexpected erosion of the spacecraft's surface during its long voyage in space.

"The deterioration of the onboard equipment ... is becoming increasingly evident," Japan Times quoted Yuya Mimasu, team leader of the extended mission, as saying.

Despite losing the opportunity to land on KY26, the Hayabusa2 mission has been a huge success for JAXA, and the new direction promises its own intrigues. Asteroid 2015 BM510 has already attracted interest; it's the primary target of a proposal for the European Space Agency's mini-Fast mission series. Scientists describe the body as a D-type asteroid, meaning it's thought to be organic-rich and comet-like, and may have originated in the outer solar system.

Around the same time as Hayabusa2 conducts its high-speed flyby in April 2028, JAXA is also scheduled to launch its next asteroid mission, Destiny+. Launching along with ESA's Ramses mission to study Apophis, Destiny+ will first make a flyby of the infamous asteroid ahead of its very close approach to Earth in 2029 before heading to asteroid 3200 Phaethon, the parent body of the Geminid meteor shower.

#725. Mashd N Kutcher Remix Rogue Traders and Dannii Minogue’s ‘Dirty Dirty Disco’

The Australian group's Midnight Mix arrives as part of a second remix package for the single.

Australian dance group Mashd N Kutcher have remixed “Dirty Dirty Disco,” the collaboration between Rogue Traders and Dannii Minogue, with their Midnight Mix released Friday (Nov. 20) via Pop Smith. Explore Dannii Minogue Mashd N Kutcher Rogue Traders See latest videos, charts and news

The funk-leaning rework lands alongside a James Ash remix, the original extended version and a Super Disco Club remix, forming a second package of mixes for the single. Related Phil Collins Says Cher Sang His 'We Are the World' Line at Live Aid After He Left Early 2026 CMA Awards Jump to 7-Year Ratings High Nick Cannon Hospitalized Amid Lupus Battle: 'Pray for Me, Y'all!'

“Dirty Dirty Disco” was released Sept. 10 as the first collaboration between the Melbourne-formed dance-rock group and Minogue, pairing her with Rogue Traders vocalist Natalie Bassingthwaighte.

“When I heard the original version of ‘Dirty Dirty Disco’ I was instantly in love with the record,” Mashd N Kutcher’s Matt James said. “What an awesome link up between two icons. The remix came together super quickly and was all about the vibes, a cut to spin late nights.”

Rogue Traders’ James Ash said the Minogue collaboration was unusual for the group. “Getting to work with the immortal Dannii Minogue, and combining her magic with what we do in Rogue Traders has led to something special,” he said. “Then when Matt reached out and basically sent me his mix completely out of the blue — I was absolutely floored.”

Minogue said she had wanted to work with the group for some time. “I couldn’t be more happy that he was digging this track and wanted to remix it and spin it in his sets,” she said.

Minogue, the younger sister of Kylie Minogue, charted on Billboard’s Top Dance Albums with 2003’s Neon Nights, which peaked at No. 17. Rogue Traders were formed by Ash and Steve Davis, with Bassingthwaighte joining in 2005; their biggest hit, “Voodoo Child,” led their second album, Here Come the Drums.

Mashd N Kutcher have had an expansive 2026, releasing collaborations with Tujamo and Darude and performing at the inaugural NFL game in Melbourne, the post-AFL Grand Final entertainment and the Sydney Marathon. They also played main stages at Handpicked, Sunny Side Up Festival and Snow Machine in Japan.

The group have logged more than 2,000 live performances, hold multiple platinum certifications in Australia and reached No. 12 in triple j’s Hottest 100 of 2020 with “Get on the Beers,” their remix of a speech by then-Victorian Premier Daniel Andrews.

Mashd N Kutcher begin a 12-week Friday-night takeover across the NOVA Network nationally on Nov. 27.

#724. Hungary eases abortion restrictions in women's rights overhaul

The reforms mark a break the the conservative policies of former PM Viktor Orban. The controversial "heartbeat regulation" is to be scrapped and women are to be better protected against violence.

Hungary on Thursday said it would ease abortion rules and ratify an international treaty on violence against women.

Under the planned changes to the so-called "heartbeat regulation," women will no longer be forced to listen to the vital signs of the fetus before an abortion.

Women will also be able to get emergency contraceptive pills without prescription.

The changes proposed by the new government under Prime Minister Peter Magyar are a significant break with the conservative policies of his predecessor Viktor Orban.

The country also plans to ratify the Istanbul Convention, a treaty aimed at preventing violence against women and domestic violence.

Hungarian law allows for most abortions to be performed up to 12 weeks, and up to 24 weeks in cases of severe developmental abnormalities. Until now, women were required to have a medical provider show them evidence of a definitive sign of fetal life, commonly understood as the so-called "fetal heartbeat," before deciding whether to have an abortion.

The controversial 2022 policy had received widespread criticism from doctors and women’s rights groups as being cruel and humiliating. It will now be scrapped.

The policy had not led to a decline in abortions and according to Magyar, had raised "serious bioethical questions."

The second major change is that emergency contraception will be available without prescription.

Further measures include changing the criminal code aimed at better protecting women, including making the misuse of intimate images a criminal offense and strengthening the treatment of victims of domestic violence during criminal proceedings.

Hungary also plans to ratify an international treaty on the protection of women which most other EU members have long ratified. The Istanbul Convention came into force in 2014 and, among other things, requires rape to be criminalized based on the absence of freely given consent.

"We are making it clear that sexual acts can only ⁠take ​place with the voluntary consent of the other party," ​Magyar said.

The government of his predecessor Orban had opposed the treaty, arguing that it promoted what it described as "gender ideology."

"We are making a clear and accountable commitment to putting an end to the era of inaction," Magyar said in a Facebook video.

Among the EU’s other members, only Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Lithuania and Slovakia have not yet ratified the convention.

The Istanbul Convention is a treaty by the Council of Europe, an international organization that promotes human rights and the rule of law across Europe and includes more countries than the member of the EU.

#723. Scientists discover a bizarre paradox among endangered penguins

A new study from the University of Otago, Ōtākou Whakaihu Waka, has revealed a surprising divide in the fortunes of one of New Zealand's least understood penguin species. Although Erect-crested penguins breed in just two remote island groups, their populations are experiencing dramatically different outcomes.

Published in PLOS ONE, the research found that one population has remained stable for at least 25 years, while the other has declined by more than 40 percent over the past three decades.

The study was led by Dr. Thomas Mattern of the Tawaki Project, which brings together scientists from the university's Departments of Zoology and Marine Science. Researchers also collaborated with the Antarctic Research Trust and the Global Penguin Society.

Drone Surveys Reveal a Surprising Penguin Population Divide

Erect-crested penguins breed exclusively on the Bounty and Antipodes islands, two isolated island groups located approximately 800 kilometers southeast of New Zealand's South Island.

To determine how many penguins remain, researchers conducted extensive drone surveys between 2022 and 2024. They photographed and counted every breeding colony across both island groups, producing the first comprehensive population survey of the entire species.

"The results overturn a long-standing assumption," Dr. Mattern says.

"The tiny Bounty Islands, at just 50 hectares, were found to hold almost as many breeding pairs (about 27,800) as the Antipodes Islands (about 29,800), even though the latter is 40 times larger and historically considered the species' stronghold."

The difference in population trends was even more unexpected. Despite their small size, the Bounty Islands have maintained a relatively consistent number of breeding penguins for decades. Meanwhile, the much larger Antipodes Islands have experienced a substantial decline.

"Comparing the new counts with historical records going back to the mid-1990s, the Bounty Islands population has remained essentially unchanged for at least 25 years.

"The Antipodes Islands population, by contrast, has declined by more than 40 percent since 1995."

Why Are Penguins Disappearing From the Antipodes Islands?

Researchers believe several overlapping pressures may explain why the two populations are heading in opposite directions. Natural predators, increasingly destructive storms, and differences in where the birds travel and feed could all be contributing.

One particularly troubling factor involves skuas, native subantarctic birds that prey on penguin eggs and chicks. As penguin colonies become smaller, the birds lose some of the protection that comes from nesting together in large numbers.

"As Antipodes colonies have shrunk over recent decades, the collective defense they once provided against native subantarctic bird, the skua, a natural predator of eggs and chicks, has weakened, allowing predation losses to increase and colonies to fragment further."

Co-author Dr. Klemens Pütz of the Antarctic Research Trust suggests that changes involving another penguin species may have intensified this pressure.

Eastern Rockhopper penguins suffered a "catastrophically" severe population collapse during the second half of the 20th century. Similar declines occurred across their Southern Ocean breeding range, likely driven by warming ocean waters. Today, fewer than 1,000 breeding pairs remain on the Antipodes Islands.

"As Rockhoppers disappeared, skuas may have turned to Erect-crested penguin eggs and chicks instead," Dr. Pütz says.

Stronger Storms and Different Migration Routes Add to the Threat

Predators are not the only challenge facing the Antipodes penguins. Increasingly powerful storms, consistent with wider climate trends across the Southern Ocean, have caused landslides that break up breeding colonies and leave the birds more vulnerable.

Differences in ocean habitats and seasonal movements may also help explain why the two populations have experienced such contrasting outcomes.

According to Dr. Mattern, penguins breeding on the Antipodes Islands migrate considerable distances into the Antarctic Polar Frontal Zone when the breeding season ends. In contrast, birds from the Bounty Islands remain closer to their nesting grounds, where the surrounding waters are more sheltered and may offer more abundant food.

These differences could leave the two populations exposed to very different environmental pressures, despite belonging to the same species.

The Strange Paradox of Schrödinger's Penguin

The researchers have named this unusual situation "Schrödinger's Penguin," drawing inspiration from the famous physics thought experiment involving a cat inside a sealed box.

In that experiment, the cat is imagined to be both alive and dead until the box is opened and its condition is observed. But Dr. Mattern explains that the penguin discovery turns the familiar concept around.

"With Schrödinger's cat, opening the box settles the question one way or the other.

"With Erect-crested penguins, it's the opposite. From a distance, without proper surveys, everyone assumed there was a single answer for the whole species.

"Once we actually opened the metaphorical box and looked, we found there wasn't one state at all, but two: stable on the Bounty Islands, declining on the Antipodes Islands."

In other words, looking at the species as a whole can conceal what is happening within individual populations. Only by examining both island groups separately did researchers uncover how dramatically their circumstances differ.

A Hidden Conservation Crisis for Endangered Penguins

The Erect-crested penguin is currently one of only four penguin species worldwide classified as "Endangered" on the International Union for Conservation of Nature Red List. Another New Zealand penguin, the hoiho/yellow-eyed penguin, shares that designation.

However, the two species have received very different levels of attention. While the plight of the hoiho has attracted ongoing public interest and conservation efforts, the Erect-crested penguin has remained relatively overlooked.

Dr. Mattern explains that the species' current conservation classification relies on population estimates from the 1970s that were considerably inflated. When the new survey results are considered, the "Endangered" designation remains broadly appropriate for the declining Antipodes population, but not for the stable Bounty Islands population.

This creates a difficult conservation dilemma. If the two populations are combined into a single assessment, the species' overall threat classification could actually improve, even though one population continues to decline sharply.

"Averaged across both populations, the global ranking would actually improve to "Vulnerable," masking the severity of the Antipodes decline, and downplaying how exposed the Bounty Islands, likely the species' last secure stronghold, are to industrial fishing."

The researchers warn that a more favorable overall classification could create a misleading impression of security. Although the Bounty Islands population remains stable, it may still face significant threats, particularly from industrial fishing activity.

"A single, ostensibly improved threat ranking is like putting the lid back on Schrödinger's box, trading a convenient illusion for the stronger protection the Bounty Islands population actually needs," Dr. Mattern says.

The findings highlight why conservation efforts must account for the circumstances of individual populations rather than relying exclusively on a species' global status. For Erect-crested penguins, recognizing the differences between the two island groups could be essential to protecting their future.

The study received funding from the Vontobel Foundation (Switzerland) through the Antarctic Research Trust and from the Global Penguin Society. The research was carried out under permits issued by the New Zealand Department of Conservation.

A new set of slo-mo videos gives us a new perspective on SpaceX's first-ever recovery of a Starship upper stage.

The company notched the milestone on Saturday (Nov. 14), when the launch tower at its Starbase site in South Texas caught Starship's Ship spacecraft with its "chopstick" arms.

You've probably seen photos and videos showing the epic snag from afar. But on Tuesday (Nov. 17), SpaceX released up-close views — a series of four slo-mo videos captured by cameras near the top of the 480-foot-tall (146 meters) tower.

"The Starbase tower chopsticks catching their first Starship. This unique architecture was designed for full and rapid reusability, enabling repeat launches and landings from the same pad," SpaceX wrote in a Tuesday X post that shared the videos, a compilation of which you can see embedded above.

Starship is the biggest and most powerful rocket ever built. Its current "V3" version stands about 408 feet (124 m) tall, and future iterations will be even larger.

As SpaceX noted in Tuesday's post, the megarocket is also designed to be fully and rapidly reusable — a first for an orbital launch system. The company plans to catch both Starship stages — Ship and the Super Heavy booster — at the launch tower, a recovery strategy designed to enable efficient inspection, refurbishment and reflight.

SpaceX planned to carry out such a double catch on this most recent test flight, Starship's 15th to date, which launched on Friday evening (Nov. 13). But Super Heavy experienced a low-fuel warning during its return to Starbase about 6.5 minutes after launch and autonomously diverted to splash down in the Gulf of Mexico.

That wasn't a huge deal for SpaceX, as it had already caught Super Heavy on three previous test flights. Snagging Ship is tougher; the upper stage returns to Earth from orbit, so it comes in faster and hotter than the booster does.

SpaceX had not even attempted a Ship catch before Flight 15. But the company managed to pull off the maneuver on its first try.

And Ship did some work in orbit before coming home: It deployed 26 of SpaceX's next-gen Starlink V3 broadband satellites on Flight 15, the second batch that the company has sent to low Earth orbit. The first set was deployed on Flight 14, which launched on Sept. 28.

#720. Physicists use laser light to unlock a crystal's hidden electrical powers

Physicists at Auburn University have discovered how to use brief bursts of laser light to organize tiny electrical regions hidden inside a crystal. Their findings shed new light on a mystery that has puzzled researchers for decades and demonstrate how lasers can influence the material's electrical behavior. The breakthrough could eventually help scientists explore faster ways to process and store information.

The research was led by Wencan Jin, the Thomas and Jean Walter Endowed Associate Professor in Auburn's Department of Physics, and graduate student Mohamed Kandil. Their paper, "Optical Poling of a Quantum Ferroelectric Metal across the Order-Disorder Phase Transition," received an Editors' Suggestion designation from Physical Review Letters. Scientists at Japan's National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology produced the crystals used in the study.

A Decades-Old Mystery Hidden Inside a Crystal

The researchers investigated a modified version of strontium titanate, a material with an unusual combination of electrical characteristics. Although electrons can travel through the crystal, it also contains extremely small regions with positive and negative electrical sides. Known as polar nanoregions, these microscopic "islands" can point in different directions or become aligned with one another. Understanding how and why this alignment occurs is essential to explaining the material's properties and learning how to manipulate them.

Scientists have spent decades trying to determine what happens when these regions become organized. One possibility is that atoms move together to produce the polarized state. Another is that the tiny electrical islands are already there and simply begin pointing in the same direction as temperatures fall. The distinction is similar to the difference between assembling a group of people and asking people who are already gathered to turn and face the same way. Because the regions are extraordinarily small and produce very weak signals, determining which explanation is correct has been a persistent challenge.

Laser Experiments Reveal How Electrical Order Emerges

To investigate, the Auburn researchers developed an exceptionally sensitive system that uses lasers to measure subtle changes in the crystal. By studying how the material altered incoming light, they were able to monitor the orientation of its electrical regions while repeatedly heating and cooling the sample.

The measurements revealed a clear pattern. At warmer temperatures, the tiny regions pointed in seemingly random directions. When the crystal cooled, however, they began adopting preferred orientations. This behavior provided compelling evidence that the electrical islands existed before becoming aligned, supporting the explanation that cooling organizes regions already present in the material.

A Flash of Light Creates Order in a Trillionth of a Second

The team went beyond observing this natural process. Researchers also demonstrated that short laser pulses could temporarily align the electrical islands, even at higher temperatures when the regions would ordinarily remain disorganized. Using an optical measurement, they were able to detect the pattern produced by the laser light.

The effect was extraordinarily brief, lasting approximately one picosecond, or one trillionth of a second. Nevertheless, the ability to create and detect this electrical alignment using light provides a promising approach for studying how information might be controlled at extremely high speeds.

Three Years of Experiments Lead to a Breakthrough

Achieving these results required considerable patience and technical refinement. The collaboration began at the 2023 American Physical Society March Meeting, where Jin met Japanese researchers capable of producing the specialized crystals needed for the experiments.

Back at Auburn, the team spent almost a year refining its equipment before it could reliably detect the weak optical signals from the tiny electrical regions. The next obstacle was even more demanding: measuring the extremely short interval during which laser illumination caused the regions to align.

"The breakthrough came in 2025, when Mohamed finally observed the disordered polar regions becoming aligned under laser illumination," Jin said. "Seeing that signal emerge was a thrilling moment for the team."

The achievement also represents an important personal milestone for Kandil, whose first published research paper reflects three years of dedicated experimental work.

"This experiment has truly been Mohamed's odyssey," Jin said. "It took him three years of dedication to complete the work and achieve his first publication."

New Possibilities for Ultrafast Information Technology

The discovery provides important evidence about how electrical order develops in this unusual crystal while also establishing a method for manipulating that order with light. Rather than simply observing the material's internal behavior, researchers can now briefly influence its microscopic electrical patterns and detect the resulting changes.

Although practical applications remain a future possibility, the experiments offer a new way to investigate the rapid electrical processes occurring inside quantum materials. By revealing how light can control these previously elusive patterns, the Auburn researchers have opened another avenue for exploring technologies that could one day transform how information is processed and stored.

#718. What have the talks with Russia and the US in Abu Dhabi achieved for Ukraine?

The first trilateral talks between Ukraine, the US and Russia in nine months have ended with an agreement on exchanging prisoners. Does this mark a genuine breakthrough and a step toward peace?

The two-day talks between delegations from Ukraine, the US and Russia in Abu Dhabi on November 10 and 11 ended without a ceasefire agreement.

The main outcome was an agreement on a prisoner exchange.

"We have agreed on the largest humanitarian release of prisoners, and tomorrow we will finalize the numbers," Jared Kushner announced after the talks. US envoys Kushner and Steve Witkoff arrived in Moscow on Thursday, where they are due to meet President Vladimir Putin.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had earlier suggested an exchange of "1,000 for 1,000" prisoners, or "1,500 for 1,500." Russia said a large-scale prisoner exchange with Ukraine could take place within the next two to three weeks.

Following the meetings, Zelenskyy wrote on Telegram that the parties had discussed security guarantees and that "the first step should be ending this war and ensuring Ukraine's security." He also stressed that Europe should be involved "at every stage of genuine diplomacy."

Experts interviewed by DW agree that the main outcome of the talks is humanitarian.

"The agreement on a prisoner exchange is already a major step forward," says Artjom Bronzhukov of the Ukrainian think tank Polityka.

Pavlo Lakiychuk of the Ukrainian Center for Global Studies Strategy XXI also viewed it as a "very tangible result." He told DW that "getting our people back is already a major success. That is why it is worth continuing."

A real breakthrough, he added, would be the release of civilian detainees from territories occupied since 2014, particularly people from Crimea, who have been held in Russian prisons for years.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Davyd Arakhamia, head of the ruling Servant of the People parliamentary faction and Ukraine's representative at the talks in Abu Dhabi, gave a positive assessment of the trilateral talks with the US and Russia, expressing hope that an agreement could be reached by the end of the year.

"I think the Russians came with extremely strict instructions, and it was difficult to ease the tone of the discussion. But the way the US representatives structured the talks with a view to the postwar situation in both countries opened up a dialogue, in my opinion, and allowed us to work together more productively," Arakhamia said at a joint press conference with US and Ukrainian representatives following the talks.

Iuliia Osmolovska of the Kyiv office of the international think tank GLOBSEC cautions against reading too much into the positive assessments of the talks from Washington and Kyiv.

"Diplomats taking part in negotiations will never say that everything went badly and that they have no expectations. Even when no results are achieved, they will still emphasize that the talks were constructive," she said. "For anyone familiar with diplomatic language, these are simply standard phrases."

Osmolovska points to a joint assessment by 71 Ukrainian security and defense experts published by GLOBSEC in the summer. According to the assessment, the chances of a peace agreement or at least a ceasefire being reached this year or next stand at just 19%.

She blames this on the fact that neither side is "ready" for genuine negotiations. Russia, in particular, has yet to accept that its objectives cannot be achieved by military means. "What we are seeing now is more of a farce, an attempt by all sides to put a brave face on things and create the impression that something is moving forward," Osmolovska said.

Artjom Bronzhukov sees the talks as a way for Moscow to buy time.

"The visits by the Russian delegation, particularly under the leadership of Vladimir Medinsky, are nothing more than an attempt to stall and sell empty promises to the US administration in the form of grand agreements, in order to continue receiving so-called gestures of goodwill from Washington, such as the lifting of sanctions on Russian diesel," the political scientist says.

Ahead of the talks, several Western media outlets reported on new US proposals concerning disputed territories. The Economist, for example, reported on a proposal to redraw the administrative boundaries of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions. However, a member of the Ukrainian delegation stressed that there had "never been any discussion of concessions on territories occupied by Russia."

Washington made no official comment on the reports.

Kyrylo Budanov, a member of the negotiating delegation and head of the Ukrainian president's office, declined to say whether Russia had used the talks to demand that Ukrainian troops withdraw from the Donbas. Asked by journalists whether Moscow was still insisting that Ukraine pull out of the region, Budanov said the content of the negotiations would remain confidential until an agreement was reached.

"The issues discussed in the talks are matters for negotiation. The only thing that matters is the outcome. Once we achieve it, it will be made public," Budanov said.

The head of the Russian delegation, Vladimir Medinsky, took a different tone, declaring that "every inch of our land will be returned to Russia one way or another." He was responding to reports in European media that Ukraine was rejecting territorial concessions.

In addition to the Crimean Peninsula, annexed in 2014, Russian President Vladimir Putin claims the four Ukrainian regions of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson in their entirety as Russian territory, even though Russia does not have full military control over them.

"Putin is not fighting over villages and ruined cowsheds in the Donbas. He is fighting for geopolitical influence and trying to exploit the collapse of the old world order," says Artjom Bronzhukov.

The expert from the Polityka think tank recalls that Ukraine was already asked in early 2026 to withdraw its troops from the part of the Donbas it controls and turn the area into a free economic zone. Such a zone "would very quickly become a Russian-controlled area," he warns.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Pavlo Lakiychuk questions the idea of changing administrative boundaries.

"Why would Putin stop there?" asks the expert from the Strategy XXI center. In his view, US negotiators are seeking to extract unilateral concessions from Ukraine "step by step" without demanding anything in return from Russia.

Iuliia Osmolovska describes the proposal as "very original," but says it would pose risks for Ukraine's leadership. Even if the Ukrainian delegation agreed to it, which Osmolovska doubts, the decision would have to be explained to the public, which, she says, is not ready to accept it.

The GLOBSEC expert points out that, following the last harsh winter, marked by shortages of electricity and heating, only 5% of Ukrainians were willing to make concessions to Russia in exchange for an end to attacks on the energy sector.

Following the meeting between Jared Kushner, US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Vladimir Putin in Moscow, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he wants to "coordinate positions with the Americans once again." No further trilateral meetings have been announced so far.

Iuliia Osmolovska believes the parties will sooner or later have to admit that the negotiations have reached a dead end. She expects each side to return to military action.

Pavlo Lakiychuk, by contrast, believes the talks should continue, if only to secure the return of prisoners. He is also convinced that Europeans "will always be there," because the issue is not just the Russian-Ukrainian war but the security of the entire continent.

Hayabusa made two touchdowns on asteroid Itokawa. Each time, the spacecraft went into safe mode.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 19, 2005, the Japanese Hayabusa spacecraft made the first liftoff from an asteroid. Hayabusa was supposed to return asteroid samples to Earth.

Asteroids are space rocks that were formed during the early solar system. We study asteroids to learn more about the solar system's history. Hayabusa (pronounced HI-uh-BOOS-uh) made two touchdowns on asteroid Itokawa (EE -toh-KA-wah). Each time, the spacecraft went into safe mode. Controllers weren't sure if Hayabusa gathered any material. But they sent the spacecraft back to Earth anyway.

Hayabusa's sample return capsule returned to Earth in June 2010. Scientists found dust of Itokawa inside the capsule, proving that it did indeed capture samples of Itokawa.

The primary goal of Japan's Hayabusa mission to asteroid Itokawa was never to be the first spacecraft to liftoff from a space rock. The mission was always aimed at collecting samples from an asteroid and returning them to Earth.

It was a hard road to Itokawa for Hayabusa. The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) launched the probe on May 9, 2003, with plans for an arrival at the asteroid in the early summer of 2005.

That asteroid arrival was delayed until September 2005 after a solar storm degraded Hayabusa's solar arrays, limiting the available power for its ion engines.

Still, Hayabusa managed to limp along its path to reach the asteroid Itokawa on Sept. 12, 2005.

Hayabusa dropped a small lander onto Itokawa, but that probe was apparently lost. Hayabusa then dropped a landing target on the asteroid, and ultimately managed to touchdown about 99 feet from the marker, JAXA has said.

During its first landing on Nov. 19, Hayabusa descended to a point just 56 feet above Itokawa before going silent for 3 hours, according to an Associated Press report. Once contact was restored, JAXA officials confirmed the probe had landed, and it eventually lifted off for a second attempt. That was the first-ever liftoff from an asteroid by a spacecraft.

"The spacecraft actually bounced off the surface a few times and spent about 39 minutes resting on the asteroid, but apparently the samplers never fired," Andrew Cheng, a Hayabusa science team member at Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory, told Space.com at the time. There was hope that some material managed to make it inside the collector anyway.

"After all the thrashing about ... there is no way to confirm that," Cheng had said. The second landing on Itokawa occured a few days later on Nov. 26, 2005.

In November 2010, five months after Hayabusa's sample-return capsule touched down in Australia, JAXA announced some good news: Hayabusa did collect 1,500 dust grains from asteroid Itokawa, samples that were jammed into the collector by the two landings, despite is collector mechanism not firing.

The ultimate success of Hayabusa spurred the creation of another sample-return mission by Japan: Hayabusa2.

That probe launched in December 2014 and arrived at asteroid Ryugu (REE-ooh-goo) in 2018. It collected its own samples and returned them to Earth in December 2020. The Hayabusa2 probe is now on an extended mission to the asteroid 2015 BM510, which it will fly by in April 2028. It had planned to land on a strange asteroid 1998 KY26, but suffered engine trouble that made that rendezvous impossible

#716. Dinosaurs may have been eating seaweed 100 million years ago

Dinosaurs living along ancient coastlines may have enjoyed an unexpected addition to their diets: seaweed and other food from the ocean. New research suggests that marine resources washed onto prehistoric beaches helped feed dinosaurs and their prey millions of years ago.

Today, powerful storms frequently deposit seaweed and other ocean material along shorelines, creating opportunities for animals that live on land to find additional food. Scientists call this process marine subsidization (MS). It is especially common in coastal environments and can become more important when food on land is limited, such as during droughts.

A new study published in Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution suggests that this relationship between land and sea existed during the age of dinosaurs. By examining chemical signatures preserved in fossils, researchers found evidence that ocean resources contributed to prehistoric food chains.

"We show that coastal terrestrial organisms in the greenhouse climates of the Cretaceous relied on marine resources to supplement their diets in a similar way that modern organisms do," said first author Dr. Clayton Forster, a geologist at the University of Arkansas. "We can identify that marine resources are passed along the food chain and incorporated in the minerals of bones and teeth of dinosaurs, crocodiles, turtles, and fish."

Mysterious Chemical Clues in Dinosaur Teeth

The discovery helps explain a longstanding mystery involving the chemical composition of dinosaur teeth.

Plants contain two forms of carbon known as isotopes: 'light' (C-12) and 'heavy' (C-13). Scientists can measure the relative amounts of these isotopes, expressed as δ13C, to identify a chemical fingerprint that passes from food into the animals that consume it.

As animals eat, this carbon signature becomes incorporated into their tooth enamel. The δ13C value in enamel is typically higher than that of the food consumed, with living animals generally showing an increase of between 11 and 13 parts per thousand.

However, previous measurements of dinosaur teeth have consistently revealed unusually high values. These readings also exceed what scientists would expect from animals that ate only plants growing on land, which generally have lower δ13C values than most marine plants.

One possible explanation is that dinosaurs, or the animals they consumed, were obtaining some of their nutrients from the ocean.

"By determining the carbon isotope composition of dinosaur, fish, and crocodile tooth enamel, we can determine what their primary dietary source was and if they were different between regions," explained Forster.

Fossils Reveal a Prehistoric Ocean Food Source

To investigate, researchers examined fossils from (once) coastal locations bordering the Western Interior Seaway and the ancient coastline of the Gulf of Mexico. Around 100 million years ago, the Western Interior Seaway was an enormous inland sea that divided North America into two separate landmasses.

The team also analyzed fossils from locations farther inland, allowing them to compare animals that lived near the ocean with those that occupied landlocked environments.

The fossil deposits formed during two intervals of the Cretaceous Period: the early Albian (around 113-107 million years ago) and the early Cenomanian (approximately 100-96 million years ago).

Researchers used powdered fossil material to measure carbon isotope signatures from both periods. They also determined the latitudes where the animals had lived to investigate whether geography influenced the results.

A clear pattern emerged. Fossils from coastal environments consistently contained higher δ13C values than those from the inland formation. Remarkably, the coastal signatures remained similar across different locations, regardless of latitude or geological age.

These findings provide the first evidence of marine subsidization in prehistoric ecosystems, indicating that nutrients originating in the ocean were entering food chains on land millions of years ago.

Seaweed May Have Been on the Dinosaur Menu

The researchers next considered what ocean food source could explain the widespread chemical signatures.

"Coastal-dwelling organisms must have eaten some kind of organic matter from the ocean, or prey that had done so. This pattern is shared from fish to megaherbivores and indicates that the extra carbon source must have been low in the food-chain to affect both aquatic and terrestrial animals," Forster explained.

For the same chemical pattern to appear in such a wide variety of animals, the marine food source would likely have entered the food chain near its base. It also needed to be something that existed along coastlines but was absent farther inland, while remaining available for millions of years.

Seaweed emerged as the most likely explanation.

"Few organisms meet these criteria besides marine macroalgae or macrophytes - seaweeds," said Forster. "Given the almost ubiquitous behavior of large coastal herbivores today to supplement their diet with seaweeds, it's likely that most of the sampled herbivorous dinosaurs were no different."

Modern plant-eating animals living near coastlines often consume seaweed to supplement their diets. The fossil evidence suggests that many herbivorous dinosaurs may have behaved similarly, with marine nutrients also passing to other animals through the food chain.

Not Every Dinosaur Had a Taste for the Sea

Despite the widespread evidence of marine nutrients in coastal food webs, the researchers found that not every dinosaur took advantage of these resources.

One notable exception was Tenontosaurus tilletti, a large plant-eating dinosaur whose fossils have been discovered at numerous locations dating to the Cretaceous Period.

Its tooth enamel contained δ13C values comparable to those of modern animals that feed on plants growing on land. This suggests that Tenontosaurus tilletti did not rely on marine food sources, even though other dinosaurs apparently did.

The difference also strengthens the researchers' interpretation of the fossil evidence. If geological processes occurring after death had altered the carbon signatures in dinosaur teeth, the same unusual values would be expected more broadly. Instead, the variation between species suggests that the elevated readings reflect genuine differences in diet.

An Ancient Connection Between Land and Ocean

Although the findings provide strong evidence that marine resources supported the coastal ecosystems examined, important questions remain.

The available fossils do not include specimens from polar or equatorial regions during the early Albian and early Cenomanian. As a result, scientists cannot yet determine how widespread this feeding behavior was across different latitudes.

Additional studies will also be needed to establish whether similar relationships existed during other geological periods, including the earlier Jurassic Period and the later early Cenozoic Era.

Beyond revealing a surprising possibility about what dinosaurs ate, the discovery highlights how closely life on land has been connected to the ocean throughout Earth's history.

"Our study emphasizes the connections between terrestrial and marine ecosystems," concluded Forster. "They are deeply intertwined and have been for hundreds of millions of years. It highlights the importance of environmental linkages across time and space and protecting them where they exist today."

Materials provided by Frontiers. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#713. Ariana Grande Recalls ‘Wildest Place’ She’s Heard Her Music Playing: ‘Getting a Bikini Wax’

The star told the story of the slightly awkward encounter while promoting new movie Focker-in-Law.

Ariana Grande has a funny story about the time her song started playing mid-bikini wax.

She recalled the slightly awkward encounter in a new video segment with Focker-in-Law co-star Beanie Feldstein ahead of the comedy’s Nov. 25 opening in movie theaters. Grande (who plays Olivia Jones in the film) and Feldstein (Samantha Focker) sat down for a casual on-camera art session/Q&A with Harper’s Bazaar in which they painted pictures for each other.

“What’s the wildest place you’ve heard your own song playing?” Grande was asked mid-interview.

“Yeah, I was one time getting a bikini wax,” she answered without hesitation, as seen in the video clip below.

“Yeah, I was, and this song came on,” continued Grande, who this week was nominated for four Grammys, including a song of the year nod for “hate that i made you love me.”

“I didn’t think she knew who I was at all,” added Grande of the woman waxing her. “I never assume anyone does, and she was, you know, doing her work at her job and my song came on.”

The pop star/actress reenacted the esthetician’s reaction to unexpectedly hearing an Ariana Grande song play while waxing Ariana Grande, and the intimate little moment they shared through facial expressions.

“And she was like, ‘And my kids love your show, by the way,'” Grande recalled, sharing that her own response was, “Oh, perfect.”

“You know, it was just very, it was wonderful. I love women and being a woman. It was very bonding,” she said.

Focker-in-Law, the latest installment of the Meet the Parents franchise and the family hijinks to come when the Focker and Byrnes families are involved, reprises Robert De Niro’s role as Jack Byrnes and Ben Stiller’s as Greg Focker opposite Grande, who’s introduced as the fiance of Greg’s now-grown son, Henry Focker (Skyler Gisondo). Feldstein joins the cast as Greg’s daughter.

#712. Euclid discovers ancient cosmic beacons from the dawn of time, shining like a trillion suns

The European Space Agency's Euclid space telescope has discovered 31 exceptionally ancient quasars, including two that have set new records as the earliest ever observed. These brilliant galactic centers, powered by enormous black holes, were already radiating as much light as a trillion Suns when the Universe was only 670 million years old, about 5% of its present age.

Quasars are among the brightest objects in the cosmos. They appear during a relatively short period in a galaxy's history when huge quantities of gas and other material spiral toward its central supermassive black hole. This process releases extraordinary amounts of energy, causing the galaxy's core to shine hundreds or even thousands of times more brightly than the rest of the galaxy combined.

Astronomers have spent decades searching for quasars from the Universe's earliest years because they offer valuable clues about the formation of the first galaxies and supermassive black holes. Finding them, however, is extremely challenging. Few galaxies had grown large enough to host such objects at that early stage, and the light reaching us today is incredibly faint. These distant sources can also be difficult to distinguish from stars much closer to Earth.

Launched in 2023, Euclid is transforming that search. Its ability to survey enormous regions of the sky and detect faint objects has already produced an unprecedented collection of 31 quasars from the early Universe, including some dating back to when the cosmos was just 5% of its current age.

"These early quasars date back to the Universe's infancy," says Daming Yang of Leiden University in the Netherlands, lead author of the Euclid discovery paper. "By finding and studying them, we can better understand how these enormous systems formed and grew so quickly - one of the greatest mysteries in astrophysics."

Euclid Reveals a Hidden Population of Ancient Quasars

Until now, astronomers had identified only a small fraction of the quasars that existed during the Universe's earliest period. Most known examples were exceptionally luminous objects that stood out because they were easier to detect. This limited sample made it difficult to understand the broader population and how these powerful systems developed.

Euclid is changing that picture by identifying not only the brightest quasars but also much fainter examples that previous searches struggled to find. Its discoveries are providing scientists with a far more representative view of the ancient quasar population, opening the door to more detailed studies of these early cosmic objects.

"Euclid is a true game-changer," adds Daming. "Before, we could only find a handful of the very brightest ancient quasars, but Euclid lets us search far more efficiently across huge areas of sky to capture much fainter light. It's a unique tool for quasar hunting."

Among the 31 newly identified quasars, 12 have a redshift of 7 or greater. Redshift describes how light is stretched as the Universe expands and helps astronomers determine how far away an object is and how far back in cosmic history its light originated. A redshift of at least 7 places these quasars within the Universe's first 770 million years.

Two Record-Breaking Quasars From Cosmic Dawn

Two objects stand out as particularly extraordinary. The most ancient, EUCL J172902.75+641018.1, has a redshift of 7.77, while EUCL J125308.55+705432.3 has a redshift of 7.69. Both are located just over 13 billion light-years from Earth and were already shining within the first 670 million years of cosmic history.

These discoveries establish new records for the earliest known quasars. The previous record belonged to an object discovered in 2021, which has a redshift of 7.64.

"This finding more than doubles the number of quasars we know of that are so ancient," says Antonio La Marca, an ESA Research Fellow in the Euclid team.

The pace of discovery is especially remarkable. Astronomers needed more than a decade to identify roughly the first 10 quasars with redshifts of 7 or higher. Euclid has already surpassed that number in just one year, demonstrating how dramatically the telescope is accelerating research into the early Universe.

"The Euclid team has taken a true 'census' of quasars at the dawn of the Universe for the first time," adds Antonio. "It's a big step towards understanding these fascinating objects on a more fundamental level."

Ancient Black Holes Reveal Clues About the First Galaxies

One of the newly discovered objects is already offering additional insight into conditions during the Universe's infancy. Silvia Belladitta and colleagues recently conducted a more detailed investigation of the second most ancient quasar identified by Daming and his team.

Their observations revealed that the quasar sits inside a galaxy filled with gas and dust where new stars are forming at a tremendous rate. This provides an important glimpse of the environment surrounding an early supermassive black hole and could help researchers understand how the first massive galaxies evolved alongside the black holes at their centers.

These quasars also belong to a transformative chapter in cosmic history known as the epoch of reionization. During this period, the Universe emerged from a cold, dark state (the 'dark ages') as increasingly energetic radiation heated the surrounding gas and ionized it (split apart by energetic light). This fundamental transition helped establish the conditions that shaped the Universe we observe today.

"Ancient quasars are rare discoveries. They're interesting in themselves, but also time machines that enable us to explore the early Universe and understand how the first generation of galaxies came to be," says ESA Euclid Project Scientist Valeria Pettorino.

How Euclid Is Transforming the Search for Cosmic Giants

Euclid's success comes from a powerful combination of capabilities. The telescope can examine enormous portions of the sky while collecting detailed images and detecting faint infrared light from extremely distant objects. Together, these features make it exceptionally effective at finding rare sources that earlier surveys could easily miss.

"Euclid's capabilities are unrivaled. The telescope combines a large area, depth, sharp imaging, and unique space-based infrared vision in a way that lets us pick out rare, extremely distant objects far more efficiently than before.

"And it's not just the telescope: the data processing is only possible thanks to thousands of Euclid Consortium scientists and engineers working together to deliver scientific discoveries, sifting through enormous datasets to identify rare, distant quasars that we can study further using telescopes on the ground."

All 31 quasars were identified using observations from the Euclid Wide Survey, an ambitious project that will eventually examine more than one-third of the entire sky.

Although Euclid's primary mission is to investigate the dark Universe, its observations are revealing much more. By studying billions of galaxies, the telescope is helping astronomers investigate the Universe's composition, history, evolution, and vast cosmic structure. At the same time, its sweeping survey is uncovering rare ancient quasars that offer a remarkable opportunity to explore how the first galaxies and giant black holes emerged.

As Euclid continues mapping the cosmos, astronomers expect its growing collection of distant quasars to provide new clues about one of astrophysics' most enduring questions: how supermassive black holes became so enormous in such a remarkably short time after the Big Bang.

PASADENA, Calif. – NASA's Voyager mission team cheered and wiped away tears here on Thursday (Nov. 19), celebrating a big milestone — Voyager 1 just reached one light-day from Earth, something no other spacecraft has ever done. The excitement persisted despite a communication anomaly that cropped up on the probe, which the team remains confident is temporary.

Voyager team members gathered for a press conference about the mission at the Von Karman auditorium here at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) — the first such Voyager event since 1989, when Voyager 1's twin, Voyager 2, flew past Neptune. The gathering served to celebrate Voyager 1's distance milestone: At 5:16 a.m. EST (1016 GMT) on Wednesday (Nov. 18), the probe reached one light-day from Earth — the distance a photon travels in one day, which is about 16 billion miles (26 billion kilometers). That means it now takes a full day for a signal to travel from Earth to Voyager 1, the farthest human-made object out in space.

"I remember in 1977 I was standing at the Cape watching Voyager launch, and I never thought I would be here today, 49 years later, to celebrate Voyager's one light-day. What an incredible milestone," Voyager project scientist Linda Spilker said during Thursday's event.

While this day and this week have been chock-full of excitement over the distance milestone, the Voyager mission team has been hard at work, as usual, keeping the two nearly 50-year-old spacecraft alive and functioning.

Unfortunately, as JPL spokesperson Raquel Villanueva shared at this celebration, on Saturday (Nov. 14), Voyager 1 stopped transmitting science and engineering data. The team has remained in contact with Voyager 1 while investigating the issue, and they are confident that they'll be able to solve it soon.

"We listen to each spacecraft every day," Voyager project manager Suzanne Dodd told Space.com at the event. Regarding Voyager 1, "we have an anomaly that is not something unseen before," Dodd said. "We do have a very strong carrier signal. We currently don't have a frame sync, so we're not getting the science or engineering data currently."

"But if you recall," Dodd added, "one light-day is very far from us. [It takes] 24 hours to get the signal to the spacecraft, 24 hours for the signal to come down, so it takes two days to diagnose anything on the spacecraft … So we can't do anything fast, and the data rates are very low."

According to Dodd, this anomaly isn't a major cause for long-term concern. Rather, it's likely just part of the natural aging process for spacecraft.

"These spacecraft are old," she said. "All of us old people have our aches and pains, and you know, sometimes it takes longer to stretch out your muscles and remember things, and so we are in a realm where we're going to see more anomalies with Voyager just due to the distance and the age."

"But we feel Voyager 1, although it's not sending us the telemetry data, it's pointed at the Earth. It's sending us a strong carrier signal, and I'm confident that it won't be too long, and it will send us data back."

And, for anyone curious how Voyager 1's slower twin Voyager 2 is faring, Dodd shared that it is doing very well on its own journey through interstellar space. "Voyager 2 is very healthy. It's continuing its mission. It has three scientific instruments on it," she told Space.com.

"Each spacecraft is basically setting a record every day for longevity or distance," Dodd added about the twin probes.

Despite the communications anomaly — and even though most of the team had been up all night to confirm the one-light-day signal from Voyager 1 — the room was alive with excitement. The Voyagers have been flying for nearly 50 years on a mission expected to last just five years, so the team was beyond ready to celebrate.

Amidst the more technical updates about the mission and its current status out in interstellar space, the event included footage of Voyager light-day celebrations from around the world. From children cheering on Voyager to iconic landmarks lighting up gold in honor of the mission's Golden Record, the Voyager love echoed around the world in photos and videos. The footage of this international celebration was enough to move Nicky Fox, NASA's associate administrator for the Science Mission Directorate, nearly to tears.

"I actually thought I was going to start sobbing," Fox joked to Space.com after the media briefing. "I think just hearing children's voices and people saying 'We love you, Voyager,' 'Go Voyager' — it just was amazing."

And Fox and the mission team members weren't the only ones sharing their love for Voyager. NASA astronaut Jessica Watkins beamed down her own video message to the Voyager 1 spacecraft from the International Space Station, sharing in the celebration.

"Dear Voyager 1," Watkins said. "As an orbiting outpost just 250 miles [400 kilometers] above Earth, we often feel distant yet deeply connected to our home planet. The International Space Station has had crew continuously living off of the Earth for 26 years, seen hundreds of visitors from around the world, and enabled thousands of experiments to advance space exploration.

"While you have been traveling into the unknown for nearly half a century, helping pave our path, together, our two journeys tell a single story of exploration," she continued. "One remains close to home, and the other reaches ever outward. Voyager 1, you have been a beacon of light, a symbol of exploration, a seeker of truth, a carrier of hope, a brave explorer, traveling further than any human hand has ever reached. You represent the very best of what humanity has to offer.

"As you reach a distance of one light-day from Earth, the entire crew of Expedition 75 and people across the planet send you our admiration and our wishes for a safe and continued journey as you begin your post-one-light-day era. There are so many amazing milestones and discoveries to come. You have a universe ahead of you, and you carry with you our collective hopes and dreams. When we look up from Earth, we will always think of you as you continue forward into the great unknown. May you continue shining bright for all of us. Go Voyager 1!" Watkins said, ending her message with a weightless backflip from aboard the station.

In concluding the media briefing, the mission team invited those in the room who, over the past 50 years (or more, with one person sharing their excitement having worked on Voyager before it was even called Voyager) have worked on the mission in one way or another, to stand up to a round of applause. With mission team members today ranging from those in their 20s to their 90s, the people behind this enduring mission span many generations.

Interestingly, Fox actually began her light-day celebrations earlier in the week. She, alongside writer/producer Ann Druyan — who was the wife of the late astronomer Carl Sagan, whose work helped create the mission's Golden Record and who took the now-famous "pale blue dot" Voyager image of Earth to the public — together lit up the Empire State Building gold.

"I was actually very privileged to flick the switch and turn on the Empire State Building lights on Tuesday evening [Nov. 17]," Fox, wearing golden Voyager-inspired nail polish crafted by her daughter, told Space.com. "That was just spectacular … I was there with Ann … we were both so giddy with the excitement of doing it … It was amazing. And then going up and standing underneath and seeing the tower was just really, really special."

While the room lit up with excitement for Voyager's light-day milestone on Thursday, the team was also brimming with anticipation for what lies ahead. As Voyager hurtles toward another major milestone, turning 50 in 2027, it remains an active science mission, and the team remains hard at work to push the boundaries of exploration with these aging probes.

"Voyager right now — the two Voyagers — they're in an area of space that we've never been into. So every single bit of data that comes back is precious because it's unique," Fox said.

"Now we're in a region where the sun's influence is a lot different, and we're in this region where we can start to understand: What is it like out past our sun? What is it like in the space between the stars?" Voyager deputy project scientist Jamie Rankin told Space.com. "We're at a very exciting time of starting to connect what we know and what we've seen, living with this star [our sun] to what is out there."

"What's next? Voyager is just going to keep on going. You know, people sometimes think, 'When's the mission going to end?' It's never going to end," Fox added to Space.com. "Even when we can no longer talk to Voyager, they're both going to keep going … So there's no end for the Voyager mission."

Chelsea Gohd served as a Senior Writer for Space.com from 2018 to 2022 before returning in 2026, covering everything from climate change to planetary science and human spaceflight in both articles and on-camera in videos. With a M.S. in Biology, Chelsea has written and worked for institutions including NASA JPL, the American Museum of Natural History, Scientific American, Discover Magazine Blog, Astronomy Magazine, and Live Science. When not writing, editing or filming something space-y, Gohd is writing music and performing as Foxanne, even launching a song to space in 2021 with Inspiration4. Yeonjun of TOMORROW X TOGETHER won best male artist. The group also made the top 10 for fans’ choice male.

Soyeon of i-dle won best female artist. That group also made the top 10 for fans’ choice female.

#709. Gorillaz Celebrate Mexico’s ‘Revolutionary Spirit’ at Corona Capital, Bring Out Johnny Marr and Trueno

The British band returned to Mexico City for the first time in eight years to headline the first day of the popular festival.

Gorillaz returned to Mexico City on Friday (Nov. 20) for the first time in eight years, headlining the opening day of Corona Capital. During the long-awaited show, frontman Damon Albarn praised the country’s “revolutionary spirit.” Guitarist Johnny Marr and Argentine rapper Trueno joined the band as special guests — and Albarn also gave a shoutout to Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum. Related Mashd N Kutcher Remix Rogue Traders and Dannii Minogue's 'Dirty Dirty Disco' Phil Collins Says Cher Sang His 'We Are the World' Line at Live Aid After He Left Early 2026 CMA Awards Jump to 7-Year Ratings High Explore Gorillaz Johnny Marr Trueno See latest videos, charts and news

Last week, Sheinbaum traveled to Shenzhen, China, for the 2026 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, flying economy alongside other passengers. The decision made waves on Chinese social media — and came up again Friday at the popular Mexican festival, where 72,000 people packed the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez, according to promoter Ocesa.

“I f— with Mexico because you have a revolutionary spirit here,” Albarn told the crowd. “This is an inspirational country, and I don’t know too much about your president, but the fact that she traveled economy class, for me, is a really important… It’s a statement, you know? So, I salute you all.”

Albarn made the comment while wearing a red beret and military-style jacket, an image that fit the occasion: Mexico’s Revolution Day, observed every Nov. 20 to mark the start of the 1910 armed uprising against Porfirio Díaz, who had been in power for more than 30 years.

Earlier in the set, Johnny Marr joined the band for “The Empty Dream Machine” and “Casablanca”; he played on the studio versions of both on Gorillaz’s The Mountain (2026). He also performed “The Plastic Guru” and “The Sweet Prince,” which also appear on the album.

Trueno, meanwhile, joined the collective — formed 28 years ago by Albarn, former frontman of Blur, and illustrator Jamie Hewlett — for “THE MANIFESTO,” their collaboration from The Mountain. He also freestyled during “Clint Eastwood,” the song that closed the set.

When Trueno shouted “¡Viva México, cabrones!” during “Clint Eastwood,” Albarn burst out laughing and kept singing offbeat as he tried to hold it together. Trueno also used the stage to hype up his favorite soccer team, Club Atlético Boca Juniors, proudly wearing the club’s blue-and-gold jersey.

Mexican singer Luisa Almaguer was another special guest, joining Gorillaz for “Latin Simone (¿Qué Pasa Contigo?),” the 2001 song originally sung by the late Cuban star Ibrahim Ferrer for the band’s self-titled debut album. Her appearance made for an emotional moment with the crowd. Almaguer previously took part in Albarn’s Africa Express project and was chosen to open Gorillaz’s Latin American tour in November and December.

The British collective also welcomed singer Kara Jackson for “Orange County,” U.S. rapper Bootie Brown for “Dirty Harry” and “Stylo,” and MC Black Thought for “The Sad God.”

Alongside Gorillaz, other acts performing on the first day of Corona Capital included James Blake, Mumford & Sons, CHVRCHES, Yung Lean, The Kooks, Violet Grohl, Jamie xx, Durand Jones & The Indications, CMAT and Grace Ives.

The festival’s second day, Saturday (Nov. 21), is set to feature Twenty One Pilots, The Offspring, Pierce the Veil, Underworld, Sébastien Tellier and Peaches, among others.
